Decentralized quantification of neutrophils in whole blood using a rapid gold nanoparticle-based paper biosensor
abstract: ABSTRACT Here, we introduce a minimal-equipment method to rapidly quantify blood neutrophils using a gold nanoparticle (AuNP)-based origami paper biosensor (oPB). The oPB consists of two main components: AuNPs confined within a polystyrene sulfonate (PSS)-coated paper reservoir and an origami paper strip optimized for both cell capture and nanoprobe deposition. The AuNPs were functionalized with specific antibodies targeting a granulocytic membrane marker and validated for neutrophil enumeration in a sample. The integration of blood cells into the proposed AuNP-based oPB and their subsequent analysis were achieved by identifying a paper substrate that enables both cell flow-through and nanoprobe transfer across the origami layers, while ensuring stable cell capture under standard paper-based immunoassay protocols. The biosensor was calibrated using mock blood samples prepared with real specimens, ensuring that pre-processing steps mimicked those expected to be applied to actual clinical samples. The calibration demonstrated robust linearity across the evaluated range of cell densities, from pathologically low to normal neutrophil levels, and achieved both high sensitivity (limit of detection: 9.2 neutrophils·μL⁻¹) and high specificity, with no interference from the blood matrix or other leukocyte subsets. Finally, when tested with clinical blood samples, the biosensor accurately stratified patients exhibiting normal neutrophil levels, mild/moderate neutropenia and severe neutropenia, in less than 20 minutes, without requiring specialized laboratory instrument for either sample pre-processing or result readout. The results shown here pave the way for using the proposed AuNP-based oPB to rapidly analyze blood cells at any point of care, enabling early diagnosis and timely clinical intervention.

title: A matrix-interference-resistant dual-modal zinc-air battery sensing platform: Integrating MXene-Pt catalyst and machine learning multimodal fusion for accurate AFB1 detection
A particle dynamics-based soft sensor for simultaneous estimation of flow rate, viscosity, and density in microfluidic channels
abstract: This study proposes a soft sensing approach for the simultaneous estimation of flow rate, viscosity, and density in microfluidic channels based on particle motion. Conventional microfluidic measurement techniques often require complex device structures or prior knowledge of certain variables, limiting their applicability for low-cost, inline sensing. In contrast, the proposed method utilizes the spatiotemporal dynamics of particles, which inherently reflect the combined effects of flow conditions and fluid properties. Time-series images of particle motion were acquired using a low-cost camera, and particle trajectories were extracted through image processing. A machine learning model based on a one-dimensional convolutional neural network combined with temporal attention and inter-particle self-attention was developed to estimate the target properties from the motion data. The results demonstrate that estimation accuracy strongly depends on the activity of particle motion, quantified by the Active Particle Ratio (APR). High APR conditions yield sufficient spatiotemporal variability, leading to improved estimation accuracy. The dependence of performance on data quantity and observation time was also clarified, showing that stable estimation can be achieved within short observation times of a few seconds. Furthermore, a dimensionless analysis revealed that particle behavior and measurable operating ranges can be systematically organized using parameters related to terminal settling velocity. The proposed method enables rapid, non-invasive, and low-cost inline sensing, offering a practical alternative for process monitoring in microfluidic systems.

title: A Golgi-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe for the detection of chymotrypsin in living cells and zebrafish
abstract: Chymotrypsin is a proteolytic enzyme secreted by the pancreas, which plays an important role in regulating the physiological functions of protein digestion, immune response and tissue repair. Herein, we designed a Golgi-targeted near-infrared (NIR) fluorescent probe (CYB-Chy) that exhibits a specific response to chymotrypsin. CYB-Chy was designed and synthesized using a hemicyanine dye as the fluorophore, phenylsulfonamide as the Golgi-localizing group, and 3-phenylpropionate as the recognition group. CYB-Chy exhibited good selectivity and sensitivity to chymotrypsin, with an estimated LOD of 13.46 ng/mL and was stable over a pH range from 4.0-10.0. In addition, the probe could be used to detect endogenous chymotrypsin-related activity in tumor cells and zebrafish and displayed good Golgi targeting with a co-localization coefficient of 0.80. These results clearly demonstrate the use of CYB-Chy as the first peer-reviewed Golgi-targeting near-infrared fluorescent probe for chymotrypsin-related activity detection, validating the feasibility of in situ detection of this class of proteases using the Golgi as a target and providing a new tool for investigating enzyme activity at the subcellular level.

title: DNA walker–amplified potential-resolved multicolor electrochemiluminescence biosensor for tetracycline detection and photocatalytic degradation
Ultra-sensitive whole-cell biosensor equipped with reprogrammed and engineered two-component signal system Agr for detecting Staphylococcus aureus
A peptide gas sensor based on pheromone binding proteins for detecting sex pheromone of insect pest Lymantria dispar
Walnut wood-mediated synthesis of oxygen vacancy-enriched ZnFe2O4 biomimetic tubes for rapid and sensitive detection of butylamine vapor at low temperature
abstract: How to achieve the rapid and sensitive detection of harmful butylamine (BA) with chemiresistive sensor under low-power consumption is still challenging owing to the lack of relevant reports. Herein, natural walnut wood (WW) was selected as synthesis-mediated biotemplate. By facilely impregnating it into a mixed solution of Zn(NO3)2/Fe(NO3)3 solution (Zn/Fe molar ratio of 1:2) followed by sintering at different temperatures, three biomimetic ZnFe2O4 materials assembled from nanoparticles were successfully prepared. Among them, the mesoporous ZFOWW-550 hierarchical tubes calcined at 550 °C possesses a narrow band gap, a high content of oxygen vacancy defects and active oxygen species. The synergistic of the above structural advantages and the catalytic action of surface Fe4+ Lewis acid effectively enhance its low-temperature sensing performance toward BA vapor. Gas-sensing tests demonstrate that the ZFOWW-550 sensor delivers a high response of 181 toward 100 ppm BA at the optimal operating temperature of 133 °C, which is 2.2 and 2.9 times that of the reference ZFOWW-450 and ZFOWW-650 sensors, respectively. Its response time of 1.6 s is the fastest among the reported chemiresistive sensors for BA detection. Simultaneously, the sensor also exhibits low detection concentration, reversible repeatability and good moisture resistance, as well as the capability for actually detecting butachlor. Moreover, the sensing mechanism of sensor to BA vapor is investigated by combining multiple characterization techniques.

title: Dual-responsive fluorescent probe with well-separated emission channels for monitoring peroxynitrite and viscosity
abstract: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI), induced by drugs or their metabolites, is a significant public health concern. Significantly, the progression of DILI has been closely associated with the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), particularly peroxynitrite (ONOO – ), as well as alterations in the cellular microenvironment. This study introduces a NIR-active fluorescent probe, MCMDC , designed on a chromene-furancarbonitrile backbone for the dual-response of ONOO − and viscosity through two well-separated channels. MCMDC is sensitive to viscosity with an enhanced fluorescence signal and responds to ONOO⁻ via an effective ratiometric sensing mechanism. It should be noted that the emission wavelength for viscosity (670 nm) and ONOO⁻ (485 nm) exhibit a large difference (185 nm), which provides two well-separated fluorescence response channels for ONOO⁻ and viscosity detection in living cells and zebrafish. In addition, probe MCMDC has been used to effectively monitor the progression of APAP-induced liver injury and for tracing ONOO⁻ generation in Arabidopsis thaliana under Cd 2+ stress. As such, we envision that probe MCMDC represents a useful sensor for advancing the understanding of DILI pathogenesis.

Thermally assisted SnO₂ LMR gas sensing
abstract: An SnO₂-based lossy mode resonance (LMR) optical gas sensor was developed and systematically characterized to assess operating temperature as a tunable parameter governing sensitivity and humidity cross-sensitivity. Thermally annealed SnO₂ thin films exhibited improved crystallinity, resulting in sharper and more stable resonance features. The sensor response to volatile organic compounds (VOCs), including acetone, ethanol, and ethylene, was investigated over 0–20 ppm at operating temperatures between 25 °C and 150 °C. Increasing operating temperature produced substantially larger wavelength shifts, particularly for ethylene, for which sensitivity increased from 0.04 nm/ppm at 25 °C to 1.23 nm/ppm at 150 °C. Simultaneously, cross-sensitivity to humidity was strongly reduced, decreasing by nearly fivefold at 65 °C and becoming negligible at 150 °C, approaching the noise floor. These results demonstrate that controlled operating temperature can enhance gas-surface interaction kinetics while stabilizing the optical response by mitigating environmental humidity effects. Establishing temperature as a tunable design parameter paves the way for high-performance optothermal LMR sensors with enhanced selectivity and operational robustness

title: Self-healing β-cyclodextrin-polyvinyl alcohol-AgNPs hydrogel as a surface-enhanced raman substrate for all-in-one selective capture, enrichment, and rapid detection of trace contaminants in food samples
Conductive MOF nanozyme-enhanced dual-mode SERS/colorimetric sensor for uropathogenic E. coli detection

Multivalent aptamer–mediated competitive control of CRISPR/Cas12a enables amplification-free electrochemical detection of Salmonella Typhimurium
From structure to identity: Quantitative attenuation-based optical biosensing of bacterial biofilms and colonies via multiparametric OCT
abstract: The global increase in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) demands non-destructive diagnostic strategies capable of verifying bacterial identity directly on growth substrates. Here, we report a quantitative optical biosensing approach in which Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) operates as a depth-resolved attenuation-based sensor rather than a qualitative imaging modality. The sensing principle is based on extraction of the optical attenuation coefficient (µA) from the exponential decay of axial OCT A-scan signals. This physically defined transduction parameter was used to reconstruct depth-resolved two-dimensional attenuation (2D-µA) maps, representing volume-averaged structural and compositional characteristics of bacterial assemblies. Unlike transverse image-texture analysis, the proposed approach derives the analytical signal directly from axial optical signal decay, enabling quantitative characterization of intact microbial structures. The resulting attenuation-based descriptors (including statistical metrics and morphometric parameters) were used for identification of bacterial colonies grown on agar and biofilms formed on stainless steel surfaces. Seven optimized machine learning models were applied to evaluate sensing performance at both species and Gram-type levels. For colonies, the platform achieved classification accuracies of 93.8% (species) and 95.9% (Gram-type). Structurally heterogeneous biofilms were identified with accuracies of 77.9% (species) and 90.8% (Gram-type). An integrated cross-phenotype model maintained a robust Gram-type accuracy of 94.9%, demonstrating consistent sensing capability across different growth architectures. This attenuation-coefficient–based transduction framework establishes OCT as a quantitative optical biosensor for rapid, label-free, in situ bacterial verification while preserving native three-dimensional structure. The method provides a non-destructive analytical gatekeeper prior to confirmatory microbiological assays.

title: Magnetic Ni-Os single-atom/nanocluster nanozyme enables dual-target lateral flow assay for ultrasensitive Mpox diagnosis
A universal and robust framework for multiple gas recognition based-on spherical normalization-coupled Mahalanobis algorithm
abstract: Electronic nose (E-nose) systems face two interconnected challenges in open-set gas recognition: feature distribution shift caused by signal drift and decision boundary failure induced by unknown gas interference. Existing methods predominantly rely on Euclidean distance or conventional classifiers, failing to account for anisotropic feature distributions and dynamic signal intensity variations. To address these issues, this study proposes the Spherical Normalization coupled Mahalanobis (SNM) module, a universal post-processing module for open-set gas recognition. First, it achieves geometric decoupling through cascaded batch and L2 normalization, projecting features onto a unit hypersphere to eliminate signal intensity fluctuations. Second, it utilizes Mahalanobis distance to construct adaptive ellipsoidal decision boundaries that conform to the anisotropic feature geometry. The architecture-agnostic SNM-Module seamlessly integrates with mainstream backbones including Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), and Transformer. Experiments on the public Vergara dataset demonstrate that the Transformer+SNM configuration achieves near-theoretical-limit performance in discriminating among multiple target gases, with an AUROC of 0.9977 and an unknown gas detection rate of 99.57% at 5% false positive rate, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods with a 3.0% AUROC improvement and 91.0% standard deviation reduction compared to Class Anchor Clustering (CAC). The module maintains exceptional robustness across five sensor positions, with standard deviations below 0.0028. This work effectively addresses the critical challenge of simultaneously achieving high accuracy and high stability in open-set gas recognition, providing solid support for industrial E-nose deployment.

title: Engineering electroantennogram interfaces through agar-based hydrogels for multi-hour recording and drone-mounted biohybrid odor sensing
abstract: Efficient detection of volatile organic compounds is critical for applications such as infrastructure health assessment, environmental monitoring, and search-and-rescue operations. Electroantennogram (EAG)-based biohybrid odor sensors using insect antennae provide rapid, biologically tuned odor responses, but their mobile deployment is limited by the short usable duration of the excised antennae and signal instability caused by drying and contact drift. In this study, we introduce a food-grade agar-based hydrogel EAG electrode for drone-mounted biohybrid odor sensing. The electrode consists of an agar hydrogel body, a conductive gel layer, and a gold-plated core supported by a 3D-printed frame. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy results supported the interpretation that the agar hydrogel structure preserves initial electrical coupling and suppresses early impedance drift in paired electrode–conductive-gel assemblies compared with a metal-core configuration. Using excised silkworm moth ( Bombyx mori ) antennae, the hydrogel electrode maintained EAG responses at > 92% of their initial amplitude for up to 7 h under the tested indoor, room-temperature conditions, whereas the condition-matched grooved gold-plated metal electrode showed marked degradation. During drone-mounted experiments, the electrode maintained odor-evoked readout under the tested hovering and threshold-triggered free-flight conditions, and EAG threshold crossings served as operational triggers for closed-loop forward motion. These results demonstrate that a simple moisture-retaining agar hydrogel architecture can extend the multi-hour usable recording window of excised EAG sensors and support drone-mounted biohybrid odor sensing under the tested flight conditions.

title: β-glucosidase as a microbial metabolic marker: A fluorescent probe for monitoring gut homeostasis and ecosystem health
abstract: Microorganisms serve as indispensable "environmental scavengers" in ecosystems and "functional modulators" in the human gut microbiota, with their abnormal metabolic activities exerting detrimental influences on both ecological balance and host health. As a key metabolite, β-glucosidase (β-Glu) activity serves as a biomarker for assessing microbial metabolic capacity. However, the current performance of β-Glu-activated probes falls short of the requirements for assessment of microbial metabolic activity. To address this issue, we designed and synthesized a novel fluorescent probe (K-10) based on a rhodamine skeleton. K-10 exhibits rapid and sensitive responsiveness to β-Glu (within 5 minutes), effectively distinguishing it from glycoside hydrolase such as β-galactosidase. Leveraging these superior properties, K-10 enabled rapid, on-site detection in soils of varying fertility without sample pretreatment, achieving "sample-to-result" efficiency. It also successfully monitored metabolic dysregulation in the gut microbiota of an inflammatory bowel disease mouse model. Furthermore, 16S Ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) and Internal Transcribed Spacer (ITS) sequencing revealed a significant positive correlation between β-Glu activity and the abundance of β-Glu-releasing microorganisms in both environmental and intestinal samples, providing direct evidence for microbial functional assessment. This study presents a promising tool for assessing microbial metabolic level via the detection of β-Glu activity, offering insights into ecological monitoring and intestinal health research.

title: A diazirine/NHS dual-anchor microarray chip enables immobilization of synthetic oligosaccharides, glycolipids, and native polysaccharides
Exploring pre-ignition source localization using a 3D network of semiconducting metal oxide gas sensors
abstract: Early fire detection is critical, particularly given the increasing use of plastics that release toxic gases during overheating. Despite its importance, there is limited literature on combining pre-ignition fire detection with spatial sensor networks capable of localizing the source. In this work, we investigated the ability of a network of 32 commercial semiconducting metal oxide sensors in a 1 m3 chamber to differentiate between three possible locations of overheating PMMA. The study also provided insights into plume dynamics and highlighted the importance of sensor placement for accurate source differentiation. The results demonstrate the potential of semiconducting metal oxide gas sensor networks for early-warning fire detection in complex indoor environments.

title: Rational design of an ERA-assisted CRISPR/Cas12a platform for rapid and precise on-site detection of gene-edited rice
Self-assembled monolayer film of Pd-modified SnO2 nanoparticles for high-performance, low-concentration hydrogen sensors
Hybrid plasmonic phenomena exploiting modified SPR plastic optical fiber chips to make ultra-sensitive interleukin-6 biosensors
A tripodal ammonium ionophore with improved selectivity and lipophilicity for potentiometric detection of ammonium ions in whole blood
abstract: Ammonium ions (NH 4 + ) are important in agriculture, biochemical diagnostics, the understanding of the nitrogen cycle in aquatic systems and enzyme reaction products of biosensors. Ion-selective electrodes (ISEs) are among the most widely employed methods for NH 4 + determination. Their the sensitivity and selectivity are crucial performance factors that are largely governed by the properties of the ionophore. In this work, we report on a new ammonium ionophore, 1,1′,1″-((2,4,6-trihexylbenzene-1,3,5-triyl)tris(methylene))tris(1H-pyrazole), a 6-fold substituted tripodal benzene derivative. Thin-membrane ion transfer voltammetry was used to characterize the fundamental properties of the ionophore, including the response to NH 4 + , ion selectivity, and binding stoichiometry. The ionophore exhibits superior selectivity for NH 4 + over K + ( log K NH 4 + , K + pot = − 2.00 ± 0.02 ) and is found to form 1:1 complexes with ammonium. It outperforms most previously reported ionophores including nonactin. Potentiometric measurements in undiluted whole blood further demonstrated its long-term stability and applicability in real sample analysis.

title: Highly selective ammonia sensor based on flame-made RuO2-loaded In2O3 nanoparticles for non-invasive medical diagnosis
Gas sensing without stabilization: Transitional information mining via mamba-based metric learning for rapid analysis
Extended foreign body mitigation for glucose biosensors via tertiary S-nitrosothiol-modified mesoporous silica nanoparticle-doped sensor membranes
abstract: The foreign body response (FBR) limits continuous glucose monitor longevity to 10 - 15 d because of chronic inflammation and collagen capsule formation surrounding the implant site. Nitric oxide (NO), a multifunctional bioactive molecule, has previously demonstrated potent FBR mitigation abilities. Here we evaluated the impact of polyurethane sensor membranes doped with a range of NO-release profiles achieved by primary and tertiary S -nitrosothiol-functionalized mesoporous silica nanoparticles (1° and 3°RSNO MSNs) using an in vitro approach. Experiments were performed using NO concentrations correlating to those known to be released at 1, 2, 4, and 6 weeks for each NO-releasing RSNO-MSN system. The NO-release kinetics and durations achieved by 1°/3°RSNO-MSN-doped sensor membranes proved effective at regulating pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine secretion, inhibiting foreign body giant cell formation, preserving fibroblast migration, and reducing collagen production when evaluated using NO concentrations known to be present at 6 weeks. Such results suggested 1°/3°RSNO-MSN-doped sensor membranes have the potential to extend glucose sensor lifetime beyond the previously achieved 4 weeks. Indeed, both 1°/3°RSNO- and 3°RSNO-MSN-coated glucose sensors maintained stable mean absolute relative difference values over 6 weeks, with 1°/3°RSNO-MSN coated sensors trending lower, demonstrating the promise of extended NO-release for maintained sensor function over time.

title: Construction of sea urchin-like Au@CdS based on plasma-semiconductor spectral coupling enhancement and its application in fluorescence "on/off" lateral flow immunoassay for zearalenone detection in grains
Shape-memory organogels with self-sensing actuation and programmable reconfiguration for adaptive devices
D-band engineering enables ultrahigh-response self-biased hydrogen sensor using a Pd/Ag-alloy-gated AlGaN/GaN HEMT
abstract: Mastering interfacial electronic structure at the atomic scale is key to breaking performance bottlenecks in solid-state gas sensors. Herein, we demonstrate that precise d-band engineering of a Pd/Ag-alloy gate, achieved by alloying Pd with 24.7 at% Ag, downshifts the d-band center by 0.15 eV relative to pure Pd. This atomic-level tuning reduces hydrogen adsorption energy by 44% and enhances capacity by 12.5-fold, as validated by DFT. Coupled with an ultrathin AlGaN barrier that enables efficient transduction of surface potential changes into channel conductance under zero gate bias, the resulting AlGaN/GaN HEMT sensor exhibits an exceptionally high response of 16,269% to 200 ppm H₂ at 200 °C—among the highest for self-biased devices—along with rapid kinetics (<30 s), excellent selectivity, and >30-day stability. In situ XRD and XPS provide direct evidence of the reversible lattice expansion and Pd–H bond formation underlying this enhancement. This work establishes d-band center modulation as a powerful and generalizable lever for optimizing metal/semiconductor interfaces in next-generation sensing and catalytic systems.

title: Dual-mode colorimetric/photothermal LFIA for myoglobin enabled by 808 nm-resonant gold nanocages
Conductive and stability-enhanced lanthanide complex electrochemiluminescence emitter and its application in sensitive detection of microRNA-21
Integrated sensor array based on vapor-annealed 2D photonic crystals and multi-responsive hydrogels for urinary biomarkers detection
Virus-harvesting electrolytic microneedle patch for on-site electrochemical monitoring of potato virus Y
Unlocking practical calibration of sensor arrays for environmental applications through a hybrid physical and machine learning model approach
abstract: Ion-selective electrode (ISE) arrays have proven useful in medical and other applications, but their use for measurement of environmental waters has lagged. Data-driven (machine learning) models are necessary to recover usable information from ISE arrays as physical models are not generally invertible, however curating training datasets can be prohibitively expensive. This work poses the question: to what extent might well-vetted physical models of the sensors be leveraged to augment training of data-driven models, therein unlocking broader application of ISE-based sensor arrays? Using a 10-element ISE array responsive to the majority of surface water charge balance and N-nutrient ions, environmentally-representative training samples (n=273) were measured. An extended Nikolsky-Eisenman model was created (residual RMSE 1–20 mV per sensor/target ion) and used to generate significantly more synthetic data (n > 10,000) than collected experimentally. Non-linear machine learning (ML) models (random forests, support vector regression, artificial neural networks, symbolic regression, deep neural networks) were trained to estimate target ion concentration (potassium, ammonium, and nitrate) as a function of varying proportions of experimental and synthetic data and increasing dataset size. The value-add of the sensor array approach increased as target ISE membrane selectivity worsened while augmenting experimental data with physically simulated synthetic data (up to 50% of total training dataset) improved quality of machine learning models for ion targets lacking highly selective membranes. This suggests that for challenging ion targets in complex mixed samples embedding physical laws into the ML training has the potential to support accelerated ISE array development with less overall experimental lab work required.

title: Effect of the electrode body material on the potentiometric response of selected solid-contact anion- and cation-selective electrodes
abstract: Solid-contact ion-selective electrodes (SC-ISEs) are important analytical tools for ion detection due to their robustness, low cost, and miniaturization potential. However, recent findings suggest that the electrode body material may influence the potentiometric response of SC-ISEs. This work investigates the effect of electrode body material on the behavior of several potentiometric anion- and cation-selective electrodes, both SC-ISEs and conventional ones. Different anionic (bicarbonate, carbonate, chloride, nitrate, and benzoate) and cationic (potassium and calcium) SC-ISEs were prepared using either polyvinyl chloride (PVC), or polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) as the electrode body material. Two types of PVC rods, different in their apparent color (dark- and light-colored PVC), were used for making the sensors. Potentiometric measurements were performed to assess the influence of the body materials. The results showed clear difference in the selectivity of bicarbonate-, carbonate- and benzoate-selective sensors depending on the electrode body material, whereas the effect was negligible for the chloride-, nitrate- and cation-selective electrodes. These findings suggest that additives present in the PVC rods may, to some extent, migrate into the membrane and slightly influence its chemical composition. Such additives could potentially interact with analytes through hydrogen bonding or acid-base equilibrium of weak acid derivatives. Therefore, considering the composition of the electrode body material is essential for designing reproducible SC-ISEs.

Synergistic Ag decoration and Mo doping in electrospun ZnFe₂O₄ nanofibers for highly sensitive n-butanol detection
abstract: Monitoring trace n-butanol vapor is critical for human health and industrial safety. Herein, Ag-decorated, Mo-doped ZnFe₂O₄ nanofibers were fabricated via electrospinning followed by UV-assisted photoreduction, introducing a novel synergistic strategy integrating defect regulation and surface sensitization for high-performance n-butanol sensing. Systematic characterizations confirm the successful introduction of Mo⁶⁺ into the spinel lattice of ZnFe 2 O 4 and the surface decoration of Ag species on the nanofiber surface. To assess reliability and reproducibility, all sensing metrics were evaluated using three parallel sensors. The optimized 5 mol% Ag-decorated, 6 mol% Mo-doped ZnFe₂O₄ (5Ag@Mo-ZFO) sensor exhibits a high response value of 146.06 ± 5.30 to 55 ppm n-butanol at 150°C, which is 27.9 times that of pristine ZnFe₂O₄ (ZFO) sensors. It also achieves an estimated theoretical limit of detection of 3.4 ppb and a rapid response time of 4 s, along with excellent selectivity, repeatability, and long-term stability. Notably, the proposed strategy delivers superior sensing performance compared with previously reported ZnFe₂O₄-based n-butanol sensors, benefiting from the synergistic effects of Mo-induced oxygen-vacancy defects, optimized nanofiber microstructure, and Ag-induced electronic/chemical sensitization.

title: Editorial Board
A double-wedge capillary latch-based sweat patch for adaptive dual-mode sweat management and real-time pH monitoring during intermittent sweating
A zero intrinsic fluorescence Cy5 probe with dual-PET quenching for highly sensitive and instrument-independent HClO imaging in tumor and wound models
Nanoengineering frequency upconversion luminescence chemosensor for diagnostic detection of hydrogen sulfide with enhanced precision
abstract: Achieving high-contrast, deep-tissue imaging remains a formidable challenge in non-invasive diagnostics due to ubiquitous autofluorescence interference. While hot-band absorption (HBA)-mediated frequency upconversion luminescence (HBA/FUCL) offers a powerful solution, the repertoire of active molecular structures remains severely limited. Here, we introduce nanoDPP-CN, a novel HBA/FUCL nanoprobe that harnesses a diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP) core for the ultra-selective detection of hydrogen sulfide (H₂S). By functionalizing the DPP core with a cyano-vinylene framework, the DPP-CN probe triggers a distinct fluorescence shift upon H₂S interaction. Crucially, encapsulating this probe within a biocompatible castor oil/Pluronic F127 matrix not only guarantees stable aqueous dispersion but actively shields the core from competing biologically reactive species, unlocking unprecedented target selectivity. Operating via the single-photon HBA/FUCL process, nanoDPP-CN effectively suppresses tissue autofluorescence, yielding a significantly enhanced signal-to-background ratio. We successfully validated its translational potential by mapping endogenous H₂S in real-time within LPS-induced arthritic joints and accurately diagnosing plasma H₂S deficiencies in type-1 diabetic models. This straightforward yet robust nanoengineering strategy transforms a conventional dye into an advanced FUCL diagnostic tool, setting a new benchmark for the high-precision, non-invasive monitoring of H₂S-related diseases.

title: WS2 nanosheets decorated 3D porous In2O3 heterostructure for ultrasensitive and selective ppb-level NO2 sensing at room temperature
Ion-exchange gold nanopore membranes for potentiometric “total ion concentration” sensing
abstract: Non-selective potentiometric ion sensors would, in principle, enable universal ion measurements, such as determining total ion concentration or estimating the predominant ions in electrolyte solutions. They are expected to offer essential benefits, including convenient miniaturization of flexible sensor platforms with reduced temperature and viscosity dependence, when compared to conductometry, which is considered the gold standard for assessing total ion concentration. Additionally, potentiometric measurements are dramatically less susceptible to changes in electrode area, whether due to electrode stretching or contamination, than conductometric (and voltammetric) measurements. Such characteristics are especially important for measurements in biological fluids, e.g., sweat, as well as in complex environmental samples. However, conventional potentiometric sensors based on hydrophobic, plasticized PVC ion-exchange membranes exhibit an inherent, hydration-energy-governed selectivity, precluding their use for universal ion sensing. By contrast, we found that permselective hydrophilic nanopores larger than hydrated ions can lack hydration-energy-governed selectivity. Here, we show that gold nanopore (GNP) membranes surface-functionalized with cationic and anionic thiol derivatives can serve as non-selective potentiometric anion- and cation-exchange membranes, respectively. Contrary to conventional plasticized PVC-based ion-exchange membranes, which favor lipophilic ions by many orders of magnitude, both cation- and anion-exchange GNP membranes exhibit nearly equal potential responses to ions of the same charge, which is the prerequisite of total ion concentration assessment. Besides offering a robust and biocompatible platform and utmost versatility in tailoring their properties through surface functionalization, we demonstrate that ion-exchange GNP-based potentiometric sensors are viable alternatives to conductometry, being also less sensitive to changes in temperature and viscosity.

title: Visualization of antihypertensive drug-induced carbon monoxide production using a ruthenium-based probe targeting the endoplasmic reticulum
Wearable SERS patch integrating spatially functionalized no-core fiber taper for versatile off-body and in-situ sweat biomarker monitoring
High-performance gas-sensor fabricated with Ti3C2Tx ternary composites decorated with Pd and SnO2 dual-type nanoparticles for room-temperature hydrogen detection
abstract: Hydrogen plays a vital role in zero-carbon energy systems and lithium-ion battery health monitoring, while its safe utilization faces a critical challenge in achieving high-accuracy room-temperature detection with fast response speed. Herein, Ti3C2Tx ternary composites decorated with Pd and SnO2 nanoparticles (MPS) are successfully synthesized via a facile approach with a high hydrogen sensitivity based on a synergetic effect. Within the MPS composites, the dissociation energy barrier for hydrogen molecules can be drastically reduced with the existence of Pd nanoparticles, boosting the ionization of active hydrogen atoms at the heterointerface between SnO2 and MXene via the hydrogen spillover effect. The isomorphous substitution of Ti3+ by Sn4+ generates abundant holes at the heterointerface, and the built-in electric field formed at the heterointerface subsequently promotes the recombination of these holes with the electrons generated during hydrogen ionization. Benefitting from the synergetic effect, the optimal response of 73.5% is obtained with fast response/recovery time of 47 s/36 s upon exposure to 200 ppm H2 at room temperature. In addition, an outstanding linearity (R2=0.9908) is achieved within a range between 5 and 200 ppm, resulting in a superior LOD of 1.96 ppm. The MPS composite gas sensor simultaneously exhibits exceptional selectivity and cycling stability, shedding light on the new perspective of high-performance room-temperature gas sensing.

High‑performance electrochemiluminescent immunosensor for the trace detection of sterigmatocystin in corn
abstract: Sterigmatocystin (STE) is a precursor of aflatoxin B1, the most potent carcinogenic mycotoxin. STE frequently found in grains, cereals, and their manufactured products. Its toxicological relevance and the absence of global regulatory limits highlight the need for analytical tools capable of detecting STE at ultratrace levels in complex food matrices. In this work, a highly sensitive electrochemiluminescent immunosensor was developed for the detection of STE in corn grain samples. The immunosensor platform was constructed by immobilizing a monoclonal anti STE antibody onto a graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) film deposited on an indium tin oxide electrode. This operates under a competitive immunoassay format using a CdSe quantum dot–STE bioconjugate (CdSe@STE) as tracer. An electrochemiluminescence (ECL) enhancement effect based on ECL resonance energy transfer (ECL-RET) between g-C3N4 and cadmium selenide quantum dots (CdSe QDs) was observed and used to create an ultrasensitive immunoassay. Under optimized conditions, the immunosensor exhibited excellent analytical performance, with limits of detection and quantification of 9.77x10-7 and 2.96x10-6 ng mL-1 (sub fg mL-1), respectively, with a linear range of three magnitude order. The electrochemiluminescent immunosensor was successfully applied to the analysis of corn samples contaminated with STE, providing satisfactory recoveries and reproducibility values. Comparison with HPLC/UV–Vis analysis demonstrated an excellent correlation between both methods. These results position the developed ECL immunosensor as a powerful and practical alternative for the ultrasensitive determination of STE in corn samples.

Guanine nanowire amplified iontronic sensing using polydopamine-graphene nanofluidics for ultrasensitive detection of polystyrene nanoplastics
abstract: Nanoplastics, as an emerging class of pervasive environmental contaminants with high bioaccumulation potential, pose serious detection challenges due to their small size, chemical inertness, and interference from complex sample matrices, necessitating innovative sensing strategies with enhanced sensitivity and selectivity. Here, we report a highly sensitive and selective iontronic sensor based on polydopamine-modified graphene oxide (pGO) nanochannels for the detection of polystyrene (PS) nanoplastics. DNA aptamers specific to PS are immobilized on the pGO surface via π–π interactions, forming a duplex structure with an anchor strand. Upon PS binding, the aptamer undergoes conformational change, exposing a downstream sequence that initiates guanine nanowire (G-wire) formation through hybridization with complementary DNA strands in the presence of K⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions. This G-wire supramolecular assembly significantly amplifies the interfacial charge density, resulting in a robust iontronic current response. The sensor exhibits excellent analytical performance with a wide linear detection range (10–10⁶ ng/L) and an ultra-low detection limit of 1.493 ng/L. It demonstrates high specificity in the presence of common environmental interferents and retains robust performance in aged plastic samples. This platform integrates aptamer specificity, graphene nanofluidic ion transport, and DNA nanostructure-based amplification, providing a scalable, low-cost, and precise strategy for nanoplastic monitoring in complex environmental matrices.

title: Crystal structure, electronic properties and surface chemistry of In2O3 polymorphs as a basis for gas sensors application: A comparative analysis with SnO2 and WO3
abstract: Nanocrystalline In 2 O 3 is a promising material for gas sensor application. However, to date, its sensing properties, have been studied much less in comparison with other n-type semiconductor metal oxides. The available information on the crystal structure, electronic properties and surface chemistry of the cubic (c-In 2 O 3 ) and hexagonal (h-In 2 O 3 ) polymorphs is critically analyzed and compared with the corresponding characteristics of SnO 2 and WO 3 . Particular attention is given to h-In 2 O 3 , that remains far less characterized than the cubic phase, but has recently attracted increasing interest in synthesis and materials characterization studies, motivating further investigation of its potential for gas sensing. The review identifies existing research gaps and highlights the fundamental properties of the material that should be taken into account upon designing and optimising In 2 O 3 based gas sensors.

title: Simultaneous multi-frequency excitation for environmentally robust 2D acoustic focusing in cylindrical tubes
abstract: Acoustic focusing in cylindrical tubes based on bulk acoustic waves (BAWs) enables two-dimensional (2D) focusing with a single transducer, but its performance strongly depends on the match between the driving frequency and the resonance condition of the coupled transducer–tube–fluid system. Environmental variations in temperature and solution properties shift the resonance frequency, making it difficult to maintain acoustic focusing. This study demonstrates that simultaneous multi-frequency excitation of a single transducer can achieve robust 2D acoustic focusing of 15-µm polystyrene microparticles in a stainless steel tube at around 1080 kHz. Temperature variation (20–30 °C) caused a center frequency shift of 13.5 kHz, which was compensated by dual-frequency excitation. NaCl concentration variation from 0% to 3.5% produced a shift of 20.5 kHz that was also covered by dual-frequency excitation. When temperature and NaCl concentration varied simultaneously (total shift of 37 kHz), triple-frequency excitation achieved 2D focusing under all conditions. The center frequency was well described by a linear function of temperature and NaCl concentration, providing an interpolation-based guideline for frequency selection. Electrical spectrum measurements confirmed that the intended frequency components dominated the multi-tone excitation. Power and thermal measurements showed that PZT self-heating increased with the number of frequency components, while its temperature remained below 40 °C. After prior characterization for fixed-frequency selection, the method operates with one amplifier and one transducer without real-time active feedback control and can be extended by adding frequencies. These findings offer practical design guidelines for robust cylindrical acoustic focusing devices operating under predefined environmental windows.

Dual role of Prussian blue in polyenzymatic biosensing systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Prussian blue (PB) films are widely recognized for their exceptional utility in electrochemical and optical enzymatic biosensors. They serve as highly selective transducing layers for the detection of hydrogen peroxide produced in the course of oxidase-catalyzed reactions. Their effectiveness and reliability in this role have been extensively reported in the field of (bio)analytical chemistry. In this communication, we demonstrate that enzymatically modified PB films can serve not only as efficient biosensing layers but also as effective anti-interference components (scavenger layer) in biosensor architectures. This dual functionality is particularly advantageous in polyenzymatic biosensors, where suppressing signals from interfering intermediate species is essential to ensure high selectivity and analytical accuracy. To demonstrate this dual role of PB, a model bienzymatic biosensor enabling selective sucrose determination while simultaneously suppressing interferences from glucose is presented. This concept, which has not been previously reported in the scientific literature, is demonstrated here using a simple paper-based microfluidic optical biodevice for the simultaneous determination of both sugars without the use of analytical instruments.

title: In-situ synthesis of Sn-doped In2O3/ZnO nano-heterojunctions for enhanced room-temperature NO2 sensing performance
abstract: The development of low-power, highly responsive trace-level NO2 gas sensors is crucial for the efficient monitoring of hazardous gases. In this work, 5 mol% Sn-doped In2O3 nanorod composites incorporated with ZnO nanomaterials were in-situ fabricated on Al2O3 ceramic tubes via a two-step hydrothermal method combined with annealing treatment. Structural, morphological, and gas-sensing performances of four sensors (pure In2O3, 5 mol% Sn-In2O3, In2O3/ZnO, 5 mol% Sn-In2O3/ZnO) were systematically compared. Results demonstrated that the 5 mol% Sn-doped In2O3/ZnO composite achieved a high response (653.7) to 50 ppm NO2 at room temperature, which was 90-fold that of pure In2O3, 30-fold that of 5 mol% Sn-In2O3, and 1.8-fold that of In2O3/ZnO. It also exhibited excellent cyclic stability and selectivity. Characterizations revealed that Sn4+ doping and ZnO compositing induced lattice contraction of In2O3, heterojunction formation, increased oxygen vacancies (37.05%), and enhanced electron transport. By integrating the adsorbed oxygen model with density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the gas-sensing mechanism analysis indicated that the composite improved sensing performance by enhancing the adsorption energy and charge transfer between NO2 and the sensing material.

Impedance fingerprinting of biofilm formation on PEDOT:PSS electrodes enables rapid detection of biofilm-associated urinary tract infection
abstract: Biofilm associated urinary tract infections (UTIs) are not routinely distinguished from planktonic infections in clinical diagnostics, despite their distinct physiological behavior and clinical outcomes. Here, we present an impedance based bioelectronic approach that enables functional differentiation of biofilm infection using frequency resolved electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on PEDOT:PSS-coated gold electrodes. To establish these impedance signatures, electroactive ( Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and non-electroactive ( Escherichia coli ) biofilms were used as model systems. Distinct electrical fingerprints were identified across frequency domains, including a pronounced low frequency impedance decrease (ΔZ at 1 Hz ≈ −1000 Ω) associated with redox mediated electron transfer in electroactive biofilms, and a significant increase in charge transfer resistance (Rct ≈ 80 Ω) characteristic of insulating, EPS-rich non-electroactive biofilms, while negligible charge transfer resistance was observed in the absence of biofilm. Building on this framework, the impedance fingerprints were applied to clinical urine samples, enabling differentiation between biofilm and non biofilm associated UTIs, and healthy controls. Notably, most biofilm-associated UTI samples exhibited impedance signatures consistent with non-electroactive E. coli , the predominant uropathogen in UTI. Finally, introducing the urine samples into a PEDOT: PSS embedded biofilm-on-chip platform enabled continuous monitoring of biofilm formation from UTI samples and their response to antibiotic treatment, highlighting the ability to detect biofilm persistence and tolerance in clinical case under physiologically relevant environment. This work establishes impedance fingerprinting as a robust and translational strategy for the detection, classification, and functional assessment of biofilm associated UTIs, with strong potential for personalized antibiotic screening and clinical decision support

Silicon micropillar chip integrated with one-pot RPA/CRISPR-Cas12a for the detection of drug-resistant bacteria
abstract: The growing threat of antibiotic-resistant pathogens, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), underscores the urgent need for rapid, sensitive, and field-deployable diagnostic technologies. Here, we present a silicon micropillar-enhanced CRISPR biosensor that integrates high-aspect-ratio microstructures with a one-pot RPA/CRISPR-Cas12a assay for ultrasensitive and specific detection of MRSA. Micropillar arrays with fixed diameters and varying heights (100 µm, 300 µm, and 500 µm) were fabricated via deep reactive ion etching and functionalized for surface probe immobilization. Suboptimal crRNA design was employed to modify Cas12a activation kinetics, enabling declined trans-cleavage and enhanced end-point signal accumulation. The 500 µm micropillar configuration demonstrated a tenfold improvement in sensitivity compared to the 100 µm array, with a limit of detection reaching 10^3 CFU mL/^-1. The platform also showed high specificity against non-target bacterial strains. These findings highlight the potential of combining microstructured chips with one-pot CRISPR diagnostics to advance next-generation point-of-care tools for infectious disease monitoring.

A super sensitive graphene/silicon Schottky junction for hydrogen gas detection
abstract: ABSTRACT Safe deployment of hydrogen as a clean energy carrier demands gas sensors capable of detecting leaks at sub-ppm concentrations with fast response, low power consumption, and straightforward integration into process monitoring systems. Here we report a palladium nanoparticle-decorated Graphene/Silicon (Pd-G/Si) Schottky junction diode that addresses these requirements through a deliberate combination of reverse-bias operation and thermal activation near the Pd hydride dissociation temperature. Palladium nanoparticles serve as a chemical sensitizer. Operating under reverse bias at -0.8 V and 120°C – a temperature regime that maximizes PdHₓ formation kinetics without entering the hydride dissociation regime above ~150°C – the device achieves a detection limit of 0.5 ppm with response and recovery times of 20 s and 90 s, respectively, at a bias-power consumption below 0.2 µW. Current-noise analysis confirms that the -0.8 V reverse bias minimizes current fluctuations and produces a white-noise-dominated low-frequency spectrum only moderately sensitive to temperature, preserving a favorable signal-to-noise ratio. Arrhenius analysis of the response and recovery kinetics yields PdHₓ dissociation energies consistent with those of dilute α-phase PdHₓ, corroborating the thermally controlled sensing mechanism. The sensing area is inherently miniaturized, confined to the narrow conduction channel at the graphene/Si edge, so that only a small fraction of the surface requires PdNP coverage, reducing fabrication cost relative to large-area architectures. The Pd-G/Si Schottky diode delivers sub-ppm H₂ detection through simple two-terminal current measurements without specialized instrumentation – establishing it as a promising, cost-effective platform for hydrogen safety monitoring in the ppm-to-ppb concentration range.

An ‘AND’ logic-gated hybridization chain reaction platform engineered on tetrahedral DNA frameworks for intracellular Dual-miRNA imaging analysis
abstract: Co-overexpression of multiple microRNAs (miRNAs) in vivo functions as a potent driver of pathogenesis and progression through their synergistic actions, holding considerable potential for clinical diagnosis. It is crucial to directly visualize and detect the co-expression patterns of these miRNAs in cells. However, simultaneous imaging analysis of multiple miRNAs in cells remains a significant challenge, which requires high-efficiency nano-carrier and ultrasensitive multi-signal response detection strategy. Herein, we designed three functionalized tetrahedral DNA frameworks (TDF@H1, TDF@H2 and TDF@H3) and dual-miRNA initiated hybridization chain reaction to develop a reliable method (TDF-HCR) for imaging analysis of intracellular miRNA-21 (miR-21) and miRNA-155 (miR-155). Utilizing TDF-based nano-carrier, efficient delivery of detection reagents into cells was facilitated. Next, the endogenous overexpressed miR-21 and miR-155 initiated HCR amplification by consecutively opening the vertex-anchored hairpin probes. Subsequently, red fluorescence signals were generated, the intensity of which was directly proportional to target miRNA concentrations. This enzyme-free TDF-HCR strategy, controlled by an ’AND’ logic circuit, exhibited ultrahigh sensitivity, achieving detection limits of 0.95 fM for miR-21 and 0.23 fM for miR-155, enabling the sensitive detection of these miRNAs in HeLa, A549 and HEK-293 cells within 2.5 h. More importantly, we achieved the successful imaging of endogenous miR-21 and miR-155 expression in living cells via the FRET signals. This result suggests a correlation between the collaborative upregulation of these miRNAs and cancer pathogenesis. Collectively, this strategy enables both straightforward execution on common laboratory thermal blocks and the revelation of intracellular details into multi-miRNA synergy, demonstrating significant potential for clinical cancer screening.

Comparative evaluation of ammonia sensor principles for SCR applications: From laboratory characterization to real exhaust operation
abstract: Precise detection of ammonia (NH 3 ) in the exhaust gas of SCR systems is crucial for complying with emission limits and for optimizing exhaust gas aftertreatment systems. In this work, two different high temperature sensor principles for detecting NH 3 intended for use as slip sensors in SCR systems were investigated. One sensor concept is based on the selective adsorption properties of a zeolite towards NH 3 , while the other sensor type is based on mixed potential principle. First, a comprehensive pre‑characterization of the sensors was carried out in a laboratory test setup to determine their basic sensitivity to NH 3 and various cross‑sensitivities to typical exhaust gas components such as NO x , H 2 O, CO, and CO 2 . The sensors were subsequently tested under realistic operating conditions at an engine test bench as NH 3 slip sensors. The results of the lab tests could be successfully applied to the measurements during engine operation, thereby enabling continuous monitoring of NH 3 slip. Post‑characterization measurements demonstrated that the ammonia sensing properties of both sensor variants remained stable over the measurement duration. Overall, both sensor principles showed promising results with respect to ammonia sensitivity, response time, and aging behavior.

title: Architecture-driven design of near-infrared probes for bioimaging of senescence in biological systems
abstract: Cellular senescence contributes to aging, tissue remodeling, pathologies including cancer and fibrosis, motivating the development of sensitive and selective tools to detect senescent cells in complex biological settings. Here we report SenNIR, a lysosome-targeted near-infrared (NIR) fluorescent and colorimetric probe engineered for selective imaging of senescence. SenNIR integrates: a senescence-associated β -galactosidase (SA- β -gal)-responsive trigger, a lysosomal localization element, and a dicyanomethylene-4H-pyran fluorophore. Upon SA- β -gal activation, the lead probe, SenNIR-1 ( meta-ether linkage), displays a NIR fluorescence turn-on response (~17-fold enhancement), enabling sensitive detection of senescent cells. To interrogate how molecular architecture governs function, we evaluated structural analogues altering the connectivity and tethering topology of the modules. Strikingly, these systematic variations revealed that linker identity and the substitution position of the lysosomal targeting unit strongly regulate the probe’s photophysical response. The effect arises from architecture-dependent control of excited-state energetics, specifically the relative ordering of charge-transfer versus locally excited states, which is reorganized upon enzymatic unmasking to produce an efficient fluorescence turn-on. Transitioning to an ortho -amide linkage (SenNIR-2) maximized the electronic coupling, yielding a >100-fold NIR turn-on, whereas an ortho-ether linkage (SenNIR-3) produced a ~9-fold enhancement but at deeper NIR wavelengths. All SenNIR probes showed no detectable cytotoxicity in normal human skin fibroblasts and robustly differentiated proliferating from prematurely senescent cells. Probe performance and SA- β -gal specificity were further validated in ex vivo models. Collectively, these results demonstrate that not only the choice of functional modules but also their mode of assembly is decisive for diagnostic performance, providing design rules for next-generation senescence probes.

Mechanistic insights of miRNA hybridization with ssDNA self-assembled monolayers on gold electrodes: an electrochemical and computational study
abstract: This work studies the hybridization dynamics of microRNAs with surface-immobilized complementary ssDNA probes. The ssDNA with a terminal thiol group was designed to allow it to form a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) on a Au electrode with low density of coverage to promote flexible ssDNA surface conformations. We characterized the hybridization of immobilized ssDNA with miRNA-4484, a biomarker for various diseases via multiple electrochemical methods including voltammetry, impedance spectroscopy, and open circuit potential. Hybridization events are monitored via electrochemical readouts of the Methylene Blue (MB) labeled ssDNA. For ssDNA without a MB label, an external redox probe, namely Fe(CN) 6 3- /Fe(CN) 6 4- was used for electrochemical measurements. Experimental results show that the MB label significantly reduced the surface coverage of the ssDNA compared to those without a MB label. The kinetics of the hybridization events in MB-labeled ssDNA show the concentration dependent heterogeneous binding kinetics. Computational studies revealed that the full 20-bp duplex of DNA-miRNA is thermodynamically favorable but kinetically slow to form. Two major kinetic trapping structures are identified, which contain bent DNA strands and may explain the nonlinear behavior and the two-step mechanism observed by our experimental results: miRNA is initially kinetically trapped and then transitions to the 20-bp duplex, as thermodynamic equilibrium is reached given sufficient time. This work provides the fundamental understanding of DNA-miRNA hybridization reactions that are important for designing electrochemical DNA biosensors for miRNA detection.

title: Multifunctional tau-targeted theranostic agent for early diagnosis and autophagy-mediated therapy in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), pathological hyperphosphorylated tau aggregates, are closely correlated with cognitive decline of Alzheimer's disease (AD), serving as an important target for early diagnosis and therapy. However, the structural similarity between NFTs and amyloid-β (Aβ) fibrils poses significant challenges for tau selective detection. We present herein the development of novel multifunctional theranostic tau-targeted cyanines for in vitro and in vivo selective near-infrared imaging of NFTs and activation of autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP) to promote the clearance of NFTs. These cyanines showed superior selective binding toward tau over Aβ fibrils, particularly o-SFVPM with a selectivity index (SI) of 5.74. Molecular docking of these cyanines with a 6-mer fibril model revealed that they entrapped inside the tunnel of tau model through hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions. Because of its superior functional properties including stronger tau binding ( K d = 7.368 ± 1.412 μM), larger fluorescence enhancement (17.5-fold), higher sensitivity toward tau (LOD = 62.12 nM) with a linear range between 0.05 - 1.0 μM and better blood-brain barrier permeability, o-SFVPM was highly viable for in vivo imaging of NFTs in different age groups of tau transgenic P301S mice. Furthermore, in vitro fluorescence staining of brain sections of 3xTg-AD mouse model further confirmed the excellent sensitivity and specificity of o-SFVPM toward NFTs over Aβ plaques. Remarkably, o-SFVPM could also serve as a transcription factor EB (TFEB) activator to induce TFEB-dependent ALP for promoting the degradation and clearance of abnormal tau aggregates in a cell model, offering promising therapeutic potential for AD. Our results underscored the unique theranostic capabilities of o-SFVPM as an effective tau-targeted probe and TFEB activator for early diagnosis and therapeutic intervention in AD.

Sol-gel derived Ni-doped SnO2 nanoparticles enabling room-temperature NO2 detection
abstract: For metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) gas sensors, achieving rapid and highly sensitive responses at room temperature (RT) remains a significant challenge. In this study, Ni-doped SnO2 nanoparticles (NPs) were synthesized via a sol-gel method. The incorporation of nickel ions substantially enhanced the RT NO2 sensing performance of SnO2. At an optimal doping concentration (5 at%), the SnO2 NPs exhibited high sensitivity, excellent selectivity, and good stability, with a nearly 120-fold enhancement in sensor response. The excellent sensor performance can be attributed to the fact that when Ni2+ enters the SnO2 lattice and replaces Sn4+, it disrupts the defect balance in the SnO2 lattice. The presence of Ni2+ in the SnO2 crystal captures free electrons in the sensitive material, forming oxygen ions and oxygen vacancies, which alters the defect balance of the gas-sensitive element and promotes the adsorption of NO2 on the SnO2 surface. This doping strategy effectively lowered the operating temperature of SnO2, enabling reliable NO2 detection under RT conditions. Additionally, the experimental detection limit of the sensor reached as low as 100 ppb, far below the threshold of 200 ppb recommended by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH). This work provides an effective sensitization strategy for developing RT gas sensors.

Cross-Halbach magnetic levitation in density-based measurement, detection and separation of microplastics
abstract: Magnetic Levitation (MagLev) offers a precise, untethered, and accessible density-based approach for characterization of microplastics. Yet, its application in multi-material analysis is often constrained by the limited sensitivity and narrow working space of existing configurations. Here, we propose a Cross-Halbach magnetic levitation device with a maximum distance of 90 mm, enabling simultaneous density measurement and separation of multiple microplastics. Using this device, we measured the densities of six common polymers of 150 μm with high accuracy. All materials reached equilibrium position within 1,000 seconds, with PMMA levitating in as little as 158 seconds. Experiments revealed that variations in paramagnetic solution concentration, particle concentration (0.1–100 mg/mL), and particle diameter (28–150 μm) do not affect measured density, confirming the robustness of the measurement results. Notably, the device successfully separated mixtures of up to five microplastics simultaneously, with density values of each component accurately retrieved post-separation. The experimental results demonstrate the device's capability for rapid, accurate, and untethered analysis of microplastics, offering a powerful tool for density-based analysis and separation of microscale materials.

Deconstructing impedimetric drift towards signal stability for a porous 3D flow-through microelectrochemical biosensor
abstract: Measuring consistent impedimetric signals under flow remains a persistent challenge in microfluidic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) due to dynamic signal drift. This becomes even more challenging in the presence of redox probes or complicated electrode geometry. Such drift complicates data analysis and undermines the reliability of the impedance sensor. As its underlying origins are insufficiently understood, drift corrections are not implemented, leading to false positives and false negatives. In this work, we investigate the sources of this drift in the EIS signal of a porous, flow-through microfluidic sensor with three-dimensional electrodes. For empty channels under flow conditions, unexpected drift was observed only in the presence of a redox probe, highlighting the central role of redox-mediated interfacial processes. Surprisingly, even in the absence of a redox probe, packed channels still exhibited significant electrochemical drift. Comparing EIS signals from packed and empty channels with and without the redox couple, we can decouple the contributions of flow, porous packing, and faradaic reactions on the origins of the drift. We hypothesize that the drift arises from the combined effects of convection, interfacial double-layer formation within the porous packing, and redox probe–electrode interactions. A new root-mean-square error (RMSE)–based analysis framework is introduced to quantify drift and determine stable measurement windows, independent of sensor geometry or equivalent circuits. This algorithm is validated using single-stranded DNA detection that clearly illustrates that drift correction in EIS data significantly improves measurement reliability, and ultimately sensor selectivity, leading to fewer false positives or false negatives.

Comparison of feature engineering and classification pipelines for E-Nose diagnostics: Accuracy and calibration transfer on a complex human urine dataset
abstract: Despite rapid growth in E-Nose research, most studies rely on hand-tailored features and rarely validate models on complex datasets simultaneously combining real biological matrices and extended acquisition windows. This work fills that gap by comparing three progressively automated feature-engineering and classification pipelines on a six-month, six-batch human urine dataset acquired with an array of six Figaro metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensor types (TGS2600, TGS2602, TGS2603, TGS2610, TGS2611, TGS2620). The manual benchmark pipeline extracts hand-tailored time-series descriptors and classifies with PLS-DA. The semi-automated pipeline generates a richer feature space through systematic inter-sensor operators, regression-derived features, and parametric inter-sensor combinations, selecting the most discriminative subset before SVM classification. The fully automated pipeline relies on exhaustive tsfresh extraction followed by data-driven hypothesis-based feature selection and XGBoost classification. Under identical preprocessing and nested cross-validation, averaged across nine sensor configurations, the semi-automated pipeline achieved both the highest mean test accuracy (82%) and overall lower variability across independent train-test splits, indicating greater robustness to data partitioning compared to the established manual benchmark (73%) and the fully automated pipeline (72%). As a secondary, feasibility-oriented analysis, we further found that richer feature spaces complicate calibration transfer via Direct Standardization, which remained effective only for the manual pipeline, pointing towards nonlinear transfer strategies as a direction for dedicated future work.

Tuning chemisorbed oxygen in Na-doped In2O3 nanofibers for enhanced formaldehyde gas sensing performance
abstract: High-performance gas sensors for trace formaldehyde detection are important for indoor air early warning and long-term monitoring, because low concentrations of formaldehyde can remain in indoor environments for long periods. However, conventional metal oxide semiconductors typically suffer from high operating temperatures and insufficient surface reactivity, which limit their practical applications. In this work, a series of Na doped In2O3 were synthesized via a facile electrospinning method. Among all samples, the sensor based on 7.5 mol% Na-In2O3 exhibited the optimal sensing performance toward formaldehyde at 125℃, delivering a high response (Ra/Rg = 87) to 100 ppm formaldehyde together with a rapid response time (< 3 s), excellent selectivity, good humidity resistance, long-term stability and a detection limit down to 20 ppb. Systematic characterization results show that Na doping promotes the formation of oxygen vacancies in In₂O₃ through charge compensation. At the same time, Na doping also increases the amount of chemisorbed oxygen on the In2O3 surface. The increased oxygen vacancies facilitate oxygen adsorption and activation, thereby enhancing the surface redox reactions toward formaldehyde. This work demonstrates that oxygen-vacancy engineering through aliovalent doping is an effective strategy for developing low-temperature and highly sensitive formaldehyde gas sensors.

Label-free SERS fingerprint recognition of salivary biomarkers for Parkinson’s disease using hierarchical silver nanogrooves and transfer learning
abstract: Non-invasive identification of neuroprotein biomarkers in complex biofluids using surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) remains challenging. To address this, we developed a hierarchical silver nanogroove SERS substrate combined with a transfer learning strategy for salivary neuroprotein analysis. The hierarchical nanosurface features nanogrooves decorated with nanosynapses, which multilevel architecture enables the confinement of neuroprotein biomarkers within the multidimensional ”hotspots” regions of its nanoscale cavities. Hierarchical silver nanogrooves enabled label-free SERS fingerprint recognition of key neuroprotein biomarkers, such as Aβ, Tau, α-Synuclein and their mixtures. Then, a transfer learning model, trained solely on pure SERS spectra of these three proteins, extracts molecular fingerprints without requiring large mixed-analyte datasets. And the pretrained model was applied to identify α-Synuclein signals in saliva samples from 40 Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients, enabling non-invasive detection without retraining, achieving a high detection probability of 0.9678. In binary and ternary mixtures of α-Synuclein, Aβ, and Tau, the transfer learning program specifically identified the target protein. All probabilities exceeded the classification threshold, demonstrating consistent recognition of α-Synuclein-specific signatures despite complex protein backgrounds and saliva matrices. In sum, a non-invasive, label-free SERS detection of neuroproteins for neurodegenerative diseases using a transfer learning-enhanced hierarchical silver nanogroove platform is presented, this approach offers a promising pathway to facilitate clinical translation of SERS technology and support the diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases, such as PD.

Functionalized ISFETs with silk fibroin films for long-term pH monitoring in cell cultures
abstract: Precise and reliable pH monitoring is crucial for in vitro cell culture assays to maintain optimal conditions and ensure experimental reproducibility. While miniaturized optical and electrochemical pH sensors enable measurements in small volumes, they are constrained by short operational lifespans, hours in the case of electrochemical sensors, due to biofouling and sensor aging. This limitation is particularly challenging for long-term applications, such as monitoring slow-proliferating cells like neurons. This work demonstrates the extended operational lifespan of silicon nitride ion-selective field-effect transistors (ISFETs) through the incorporation of crystalline silk fibroin layers. Silk fibroin, known for its thermal and chemical stability, biocompatibility, and filtering properties, was crystallised onto ISFETs to form robust and stable films. The silk-modified ISFETs retained a pH sensitivity of 51 ± 2 mV/pH, exhibited high precision, comparable to bare ISFETs (Willmott’s index of agreement >0.99), while the drift was reduced (from 4.0 mV/h for bare ISFETs to below 1 mV/h for silk-fibroin ISFETs). When implemented in cell culture chambers, the reduced fouling effect on silk-modified sensors enabled continuous pH monitoring for almost 8 days (182 h) without recalibration or cleaning, significantly surpassing the 8-hour continuous operational lifetime of bare ISFETs. The integration of silk fibroin into ISFETs addresses critical challenges of sensor drift and aging, enabling durable and reliable long-term pH monitoring in small sample volumes. These advances have broad implications for cell culture studies, clinical diagnostics, and wearable sensing applications.

title: A Golgi-targeting NIR fluorescence-based probe for the detection of cysteine in living cells and mice
abstract: Cysteine (Cys) plays a vital role in the biological processes within cells and is closely associated with the proper function of the Golgi apparatus (GA). At present, highly selective and sensitive fluorescent probes, especially near-infrared (NIR) fluorescent probes for the specific detection of Cys in the Golgi apparatus have not been reported. Within this research, we developed a Golgi-targeting NIR fluorescence probe ( LGB-Cys ) for the detection of Cys based on an intermolecular charge transfer (ICT) mechanism, with a hemicyanine skeleton as the fluorophore, an acrylate as the response unit, and a p -aminobenzene sulfonamide as the GA-targeting group. In the absence of Cys, the acrylate group inhibits the ICT effect and quenches the fluorescence of the probe. However, upon the addition of Cys, the ICT process was recovered accompanied by a significant NIR emission enhancement at 705 nm due to the cleavage of acrylate. LGB-Cys exhibits the advantages of high selectivity, strong anti-interference ability, and high sensitivity (LOD = 0.134 μM) for Cys detection. Significantly, LGB-Cys was successfully used to image endogenous and exogenous Cys in living cells and to evaluate the oxidative stress of GA. Moreover, LGB-Cys could be applied for monitoring of Cys fluctuations in normal and HepG-2 xenograft tumor mice.

Chiral binary matrix recognition and sweat SERS biosensing via tunable plasmonic-MOF nanocavities for phenylalanine enantiomers
abstract: The integration of chiral recognition with plasmonic enhancement in a single nanostructure remains a significant challenge for enantioselective biosensing. Here, we report a general ligand competition growth strategy for the controllable synthesis of different gold nanoparticles (spheres, rods, cubes, trisoctahedron) encapsulated within chiral L/D-histidine-incorporated ZIF-8 shells (AuNPs@L/D-His-ZIF). This strategy enables precise tuning of the MOF shell thickness, which governs the nanogap in a nanoparticle-on-mirror (NPoM) plasmonic nanocavity. The resulting architecture supports a chiral binary matrix recognition surface-enhanced Raman scattering (CBMR-SERS) mechanism, where the chiral MOF shell selectively encodes enantiomers into distinct spatial conformations through synergistic geometry-electrostatics complementarity (validated by DFT calculations), while the plasmonic nanocavity decodes these orientations into amplified spectral fingerprints via orientation-dependent enhancement (confirmed by the correlation between experimental SERS signatures and computed molecular orientations). The platform enables ultrasensitive, selective, and quantitative discrimination of L- and D-phenylalanine in artificial sweat, achieving detection limits at the sub-micromolar level. This work provides a versatile strategy for designing chiral-plasmonic hybrids, which holds potential for enabling non-invasive and enantioselective metabolite monitoring, and may ultimately contribute to future advances in chirality-based biosensing and biomedical diagnostics.

Smartphone-assisted signal-on fluorescence sensor for Al3 + and Bi3+ detection using Tb-MOF nanosheets with site-selective recognition
abstract: On-site detection of toxic metal ions in industrial solid waste leachates is crucial for environmental monitoring and public health protection. Herein, an ultrathin benzothiadiazole-functionalized Tb-MOF nanosheet-based (Tb-BTDI-S) fluorescence sensing platform is developed for the rapid and on-site detection of Al3+ and Bi3+. Tb-BTDI-S features a layered framework and exhibits excellent stability across various solutions and a wide pH range, enabling its application in harsh environments. Tb-BTDI-S displays a rapid “turn-on” fluorescence response toward Al3+ and Bi3+ with detection limits of 0.066 μM and 0.032 μM, respectively. Notably, distinct fluorescence color changes allow the selective detection of the two ions. Based on the well-defined single-crystal structure, mechanistic investigations combining spectroscopic analysis and density functional theory calculations reveal that Al3+ and Bi3+ interact with different coordination sites within the framework, resulting in distinct fluorescence responses. A smartphone-assisted visual sensing platform is further constructed and successfully applied to the detection of Al3+ and Bi3+ in real water samples and industrial solid wastes. The results are consistent with ICP-based methods, demonstrating the reliability and practical applicability of the proposed system for on-site analysis. This study highlights a site-selective coordination strategy for selective fluorescence sensing and offers new insights into the rational design of MOF-based sensors for real-world applications.

Automated workflow for ion-selective electrodes via mixed-ion inference
abstract: Selective electrochemical extraction of Li + from brines requires repeated solution exchange and quantitative tracking of Li + /Na + composition across capture and release steps. Here, we develop an automated platform that couples lithium manganese oxide-based electrochemical Li + extraction, programmable fluid handling, and paired Li + /Na + ion-selective electrode analysis. To enable quantification in mixed solutions, established pure-ion, separate-solution, and fixed-interference characterization is combined with a physically interpretable dual-sensor model trained across mixed LiCl/NaCl compositions. Rather than evaluating sensor performance through a single selectivity coefficient, the model is tested directly through simultaneous recovery of Li + and Na + concentrations within the experimentally calibrated composition domain. The platform automates solution delivery, electrochemical capture, washing, release, sample collection, and subsequent at-line potentiometric quantification over repeated extraction cycles, enabling cycle-resolved determination of Li + /Na + separation performance. This application-driven workflow connects automated electrochemical separation with mixed-ion composition inference and provides a transparent route toward autonomous evaluation and optimization of Li + recovery processes.
