A dual-targeted probe of mitochondria and lysosomes based on fluorescence lifetime imaging for visualizing cellular damage and autophagy processes
abstract: The dynamic interplay between mitochondria and lysosomes, particularly through the process of mitophagy, serves as a pivotal mechanism for sustaining cellular homeostasis. Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) offers a powerful tool to probe intracellular biophysical properties with nanoscale resolution. Herein, a dual-targeted probe (QNN) of mitochondria and lysosomes based on fluorescence lifetime imaging for visualizing cellular damage and autophagy was reported. QNN adopts a typical D-π-A structure, with N-alky-pyridinium cation as acceptor which also facilitates efficient aqueous solubility and mitochondria targeting. Especially, benefiting from the auxiliary terminal -NH₃⁺ moiety, QNN exhibits exceptional pH sensitivity and enables precise discrimination between the strongly acidic lysosomal lumen and the weakly basic mitochondrial matrix with nanosecond-level resolution via FLIM. This capability allows for tracing cellular damage processes and real-time monitoring of fluorescence lifetime changes in mitochondria and lysosomes during autophagy. This work establishes a novel method for visualizing and quantitatively analyzing lifetime alterations associated with cellular injury, while also providing fresh insights into the crosstalk between mitochondria and lysosomes during autophagy.

Reflective humidity and temperature sensor based on lateral-integration fiber with the rod-in-tube configuration
abstract: A reflective laterally integrated dual-channel surface plasmon resonance (SPR) sensor based on a thin-coreless-fiber (TCLF) embedded hollow-core-fiber (HCF), i.e. rod-in-tube configuration, is proposed for simultaneous measurement of humidity and temperature. Two distinguishable SPR-influenced spectral features are generated within the 4-mm sensing length. For the selected 5-cycle device, Channel 1 is tracked by the dip minimum, whereas Channel 2 is tracked by the center wavelength of an inter-dip peak formed by the overlap of the neighboring spectral features. Graphene oxide/magnetic graphene oxide (GO/MGO) multilayers are used to measure humidity response, while polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) offers stable thermo-optical properties for temperature measurement. The humidity sensitivity of Channel 1 is 0.15 nm/%RH (28–88%RH), showing a pronounced enhancement above ~90%RH. In contrast, Channel 2 exhibits a strong temperature sensitivity of -1.67 nm/°C with only a weak humidity dependence (0.048 nm/%RH). Within the experimentally validated linear calibration range (28–88%RH), humidity and temperature are decoupled using a sensitivity-matrix method with errors of [-1.77%RH, +0.94 °C] (50%RH@20 °C) and [-3.59%RH, -0.74 °C] (60%RH@30 °C). This miniaturized dual-channel strategy offers a practical route to temperature-compensated humidity sensing and to compact dual-parameter fiber laterally integrated sensors.

title: Low-frequency segmented-flow microfluidics for biphasic chemical sensing
abstract: Droplet microfluidics with droplet generation frequencies of several hundred hertz and droplet volumes below 1 nL has previously been reported for biphasic chemical sensing based on oil sensors. However, tracking fluorescence from these rapidly moving subnanoliter droplets typically requires highly sophisticated optical instrumentation, such as laser-scanning confocal microscopy. In this work, we implement oil-based chemical sensing in segmented-flow microfluidics with operating frequencies below 20 Hz and segment volumes of tens to hundreds of nanoliters. The lower segment generation frequency and larger segment size enable straightforward interrogation using a compact custom-built optical detector consisting of a laser excitation source and a photon counter. Commercial plastic tee assemblies and perfluorinated tubing are employed in place of PDMS microchannels to minimize channel swelling as well as chemical adsorption and absorption. The self-contained sensing platform is demonstrated for biphasic detection of potassium ions, albumin, and hydrogen peroxide based on mechanisms including analyte-induced deprotonation of a hydrophobic pH indicator, analyte-induced back extraction of a fluorescent dye, and reaction of the analyte with a fluorescent probe. The system is compatible with oil sensors containing optical reporters over a wide concentration range from micromolar to near-millimolar levels. Using potassium ion sensing as a model system, we further demonstrate plasma analysis and real-time tracking of stepwise concentration changes in continuously aspirated samples. This low-frequency segmented-flow microfluidic sensing platform combined with a simple optical detector paves the way for bedside chemical monitoring in biological fluids.

Dual-mode paper-based epidermal microfluidics for sweat rate normalized chloride sensing
abstract: In resource-limited clinical settings, sweat chloride testing frequently departs from standardized protocols, leading to unreliable measurements and elevated false-negative rates. A central contributor to this failure is the lack of a unified, passive device that enables efficient sweat collection, quantitative chloride measurement, and sweat-rate normalization. Here we report a dual-mode paper-based epidermal microfluidic sensor that enables sweat-rate–normalized chloride analysis by integrating real-time sweat-volume quantification with distance-based and colorimetric chloride sensing in a fully passive skin-conformal patch. The laser-engraved paper microfluidic channel quantifies sweat volume with a sensitivity of 6.541 mm.µL⁻1 and a detection limit of 0.98 µL for localized sweat-rate estimation. In parallel, distance-based chloride sensing based on reverse Mohr chemistry provides a linear response across 0–100 mmol.l⁻1 with a sensitivity of 24.768 mm.mM⁻1 and a limit of detection of 0.094 mmol.l⁻1, while companion colorimetric zones enable rapid visual classification under low-sweat conditions using smartphone imaging. The device shows high repeatability (CV = 1.84%), selectivity against common sweat interferents, and storage stability for up to 71 days (CV = 9.25%). Pilot on-body measurements capture dynamic sweat chloride changes during exercise and electrolyte modulation, highlighting the value of sweat-rate normalization for physiologically meaningful interpretation. With an estimated material cost of less than USD 0.02 per device, this platform provides a scalable approach to sweat chloride testing in resource-limited settings.

Nanoporous interferometers for assessing DogTag/DogCatcher chemistry affinity
abstract: This study presents the development of a sensing tool for real-time binding assessment between DogCatcher and DogTag linkers—biochemical functional groups for site-specific protein labeling and conjugation. The system combines nanoporous anodic alumina based Fabry-Pérot interferometers (NAA–FPIs) functionalized with DogCatcher-labelled green fluorescent protein (GFP) and reflectometric interference spectroscopy (RIfS). Protein-modified NAA–FPI platforms were exposed to analytical solutions of GFP-DogTag of different concentrations, from 15 to 100 μg mL –1 . Dynamic changes in the effective optical thickness of protein-modified NAA–FPIs in response to GFP-DogTag were assessed in real time with the objective of evaluating the binding kinetics, affinity, and mechanism. The effective optical thickness of GFP-DogCatcher-modified NAA–FPI structures underwent significant changes upon exposure to GFP-DogTag protein, exhibiting a strong affinity. The selectivity of the system was also assessed by exposing these thin films to analytical solutions of interfering biomolecules. The sensor achieved a sensitivity of 0.56 nm μg mL –1 and a low limit of detection of 9.2 μg mL –1 , with excellent linearity. This system is a promising complement to other detection systems used to assess affinity between biomolecules, expanding our understanding of how this novel class of biomolecules interact in a confined space—with potential implications across a range of biomolecular applications.

Bay-functionalized perylene diimides combined with time-series classification for rapid trace detection of illicit drugs
abstract: Luminescent sensor arrays combined with machine learning have been demonstrated as a promising strategy for rapidly and selectively detecting chemicals of interest. However, the real-time identification of analytes over a wide concentration/quantity range remains a challenge for the field. Here, we report a family of perylene diimide derivatives bearing different bay substituents, which were selected to modulate their ionization potentials for the detection of illicit drugs. Thin films of the perylene diimides exhibited different changes in their luminescence when exposed to illicit drugs and commonly used medicines. These differences in luminescence change were used in conjunction with a time-series classification algorithm— k -nearest neighbors with dynamic time warping to show that a combination of sensing materials could be selected to allow differentiation between five illicit drugs (methamphetamine•HCl, 3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine•HCl, cocaine•HCl, fentanyl•HCl, tetrahydrocannabinol) and three non-illicit drugs (aspirin, paracetamol, and caffeine) with a mean accuracy of 94.1% after 17 second exposures to the analytes for amounts ranging from 0.1 μg to 10 μg.

Nanocage-mediated enzyme stabilization: The effect of size and charge
abstract: Enzymes are tools utilised in many scientific disciplines. The specific protein employed in each area depends on its specific activity, as well as its stability over time. These properties depend on the enzyme itself, as well as the surrounding environment. The outer boundary, being cellular crowding, immobilization, or synthetic encapsulation, modulates both stability and accessibility by imposing confinement and regulating molecular diffusion. Thus, enzyme stabilization across disciplines is less about modifying the protein alone, mainly on the precise engineering of the spatial and physicochemical properties of its environment to balance protection with functional accessibility. Here, we present a study describing the stabilization of a protein when enclosed in a solid nano environment. This work focusses on the physicochemical characteristics of the nanocavity to be used for the immobilization and stabilization of proteins for use in biotechnology applications, such as biosensors. It is shown that inclusion in a nanocage decreases the energy of the system, thus inducing stabilization effect. This stabilization depends on both the size and surface charge of the two systems. Based on these results, the charge type and density of the cage must be controlled for optimum protein stabilization.

abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a highly virulent and transmissible pathogen posing a severe threat to food safety and public health in the food chain. Herein, we developed a tri-mode (colorimetric, electrochemical and photothermallateral) flow assay for MRSA analysis using deactivated phage-modified strips and ZIF-67@MB-PDA-AuNPs-Porcine IgG (ZMPAP) probes. MRSA formed a sandwich structure with immobilized phage and ZMPAP. Total MRSA was detected through colorimetric and photothermal modes with LODs of 103 and 102 CFU/mL. Laser-induced hydroxyl radicals from ZMPAP lysed viable MRSA; supernatant MB was electrochemically measured via a portable smartphone device, achieving viable MRSA quantification at 10 CFU/mL. This assay was applied to food samples (i.e., cake, milk, lemon juice, fish) within 50 min, with spiked recoveries of 94%-106% and RSDs of 1.3%-9.3%. It provides a promising on-site method for rapid viability evaluation and quantification of MRSA in food samples.

Strain-engineered active site migration and machine learning-assisted NO2 recognition in UV-activated Cs-doped WO3-x nanosheets with operando mechanistic insights
abstract: Pristine metal oxide gas sensors often suffer from poor selectivity and limited polarizability. To overcome these bottlenecks, oxygen vacancy-rich 2D ultrathin Cs-doped WO3-x nanosheets were synthesized via a solvothermal method. Advanced characterizations (KPFM, UPS, and TAS) confirmed that optimal Cs doping (0.08 mol%) optimizes the surface work function and drastically prolongs the photo-generated carrier lifetime (τ_3 = 40.45 ns), maximizing UV-excited charge separation. Consequently, under 365 nm UV illumination at 175℃, the sensor exhibited an ultra-high response of 118.4 to 10 ppm NO2, a 2.41 ppb limit of detection, ultra-fast kinetics (10 s/7 s response/recovery), superior immunity to moisture interference (stable across a 30% to 90% RH gradient), and robust 30-day long-term stability. To resolve cross-selectivity limitations, a machine learning model integrating Random Forest (RF) feature extraction and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) was deployed, achieving 98.8% recognition accuracy in multi-component gas mixtures. Mechanistically, in-situ/operando Raman Two-Dimensional Correlation Spectroscopy (2D-COS) and Density Functional Theory (DFT) revealed that steric hindrance from large Cs+ ions induces localized W-O lattice strain while effectively eliminating surface moisture side reactions. This strain creates distorted sites with ultra-high adsorption energy (-1.3538 eV), driving a ”complete migration” of NO2 active adsorption sites away from the intrinsic lattice. By coupling strain-engineered active site migration with artificial intelligence, this work provides a powerful blueprint for the next generation of highly selective, intelligent gas sensors.

abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) serves as a crucial gaseous signaling molecule within plants, playing a vital role in regulating growth and development as well as various stress responses. Thus, it is of great importance to develop an effective fluorescent probe for detecting dynamic changes of H 2 S in plants. With this research, we developed a novel near-infrared fluorescent probe CTH-OH-NO 2 . CTH-OH-NO 2 that possess the characteristics of large Stokes shift (>100 nm), good water solubility, and high selectivity. Significantly, CTH-OH-NO 2 successfully achieved real-time fluorescence imaging of endogenous and exogenous H 2 S in multiple plant models such as onion inner epidermis, soybean stem segments, hydroponic soybean roots, tobacco roots and hydroponic wheat roots. Notably, CTH-OH-NO 2 enabled whole-plant imaging of H 2 S in mung bean and peanut plants, as well as co-localization imaging of mitochondria in wheat root systems. Furthermore, CTH-OH-NO 2 exhibits good monitoring performance for H 2 S level changes in zebrafish models. This research provides a rapid and effective tool for the dynamic monitoring of H 2 S in plants and zebrafish.

abstract: The rapid and accurate identification of organophosphorus pesticides (OPs) is crucial for ensuring food safety. However, the discrimination of structurally similar pesticide analogues across varying concentrations remains a formidable challenge. In this work, a three-channel sensor array integrating dual-colorimetric and photothermal responses was developed using performance-optimized Au/MIL-100(Fe) nanozyme as recognition unit for the precise detection and intelligent discrimination of OPs. Mechanistic studies revealed that OPs inhibit catalytic activity by binding to the active centers of the nanozymes through coordination, thereby generating distinct signal patterns. Based on this response feature, a concentration-independent recognition model was established using artificial neural networks (ANN), achieving nearly 100% accurate identification of five types of OPs. The sensor array reached a picomolar (pM) limit of detection, and maintained excellent anti-interference capability and stability in complex matrices (tap water, cabbage, and peaches), offering a versatile tool for high-throughput, intelligent pesticide residue screening.

Enabling intelligent packaging through nanoporous membrane-based optical oxygen sensing
abstract: Compromised packaging permits ambient gases, particularly oxygen (O2), to infiltrate sealed environments, accelerating the degradation of O2-sensitive products and shortening their shelf life. Consequently, intelligent packaging systems that incorporate gas sensors to monitor O2 ingress have attracted significant attention. However, many existing O2-sensing technologies for smart packaging still face limitations, such as insufficient sensitivity, limited long-term stability, and complex operational requirements, highlighting the need for simpler, highly sensitive, and robust sensing approaches. In this study, an improved optical O2 sensor based on nanoporous anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) membranes is developed for sensitive O2 monitoring within packaging systems. The sensing mechanism relies on the phosphorescent properties of palladium tetrakis (4-carboxyphenyl) porphyrin (PdTCPP), which is immobilized in a sol–gel matrix and dynamically spin-coated onto the nanoporous membrane to form a stable and hydrophobic O2-responsive layer. During in-package testing, the optimized sensor exhibited a response (I0/I25, where I0 corresponds to 0% O2 and I25 to 25% O2) of 96.2, demonstrating its excellent sensitivity. The sensor also displayed a clear dynamic response to low levels of O2 when integrated inside a package, confirming its capability for real-time monitoring. Photostability testing revealed minimal signal decay (~3.2%), indicating excellent stability for practical smart-packaging applications.

Solid-state electrochemical sensor for hydrogen isotopes. Part II: Dual-mode simultaneous quantification of H2 and D2 in gas mixtures
abstract: Achieving effective fusion energy generation on Earth necessitates precise quantification of deuterium and tritium fuel. This is critical in various stages of the reaction process in Tokamak-type reactors, such as ITER or EU-DEMO. Accurate, rapid, and reliable measurement of tritium in the Tritium Extraction System (TES) and determining the proportions of deuterium and tritium in the fuel cycle system are particularly important. However, due to the significant similarities between these isotopes, current measurement tools reported in bibliography face challenges in distinguishing them when mixed. Electrochemical sensors based on proton-conducting materials exhibit high sensitivity and can operate at temperatures up to 1000°C. These materials have shown proton, deuteron, and triton conductivity, making them suitable for hydrogen quantification under the conditions of the TES and fuel cycle systems.,In the present work, it is proposed a combined potentiometric and amperometric sensor to be able to quantify hydrogen and deuterium simultaneously from a mixture of both. The device was tested at 500°C in mixed hydrogen and deuterium atmospheres, demonstrating the feasibility of simultaneous isotope quantification.

title: 3D-printed and in situ grown lanthanide MOF sensor array toward colorimetric profiling of volatile organic compounds
abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are attractive optical sensing materials, yet their intrinsic frangibility and poor processability have hindered the fabrication of macro-scale optical device. Herein, a colorimetric sensor array (CSA) is designed by in situ growing and assembling lanthanide MOF (Isg-LnMOF) on a 3D-printed frame for the identification and detection of eight volatile organic compounds (VOCs). The 3D-printed frame was fabricated by a precursor ink containing organic ligands, alginate, deprotonation agent and commercial resins, and then immersed in a lanthanide ion solution to trigger in situ growth and assembly of LnMOF (Ln=Tb, Eu, Sm) through ion coordination and chelation. Compared to LnMOFs synthesized via various assembly methods, Isg-LnMOF exhibits a dense and uniform morphology, enhanced stability, and superior reproducibility (RSD=1.0-1.5%). Principal component analysis (PCA) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) are employed for classification of eight VOCs and quantitative analysis of individual VOCs, respectively. The Isg-LnMOF CSA can unambiguously identify the eight VOCs, and achieves the detection limits of 2.6-5.1 ppm. The CSA also successfully discriminates binary VOCs mixtures and a simulated ternary industrial exhaust (acetone/benzene/toluene), with distinct clustering in PCA space. This demonstrates its potential as a colorimetric sensing platform for VOCs monitoring applications, including industrial emission control, indoor air quality assessment, and occupational exposure monitoring.

High-throughput size-selective separation of microalgae and bacteria using low-concentration hyaluronic acid-based viscoelastic microfluidics
abstract: Efficient separation of algae and bacteria is a critical step in biomedical, chemical, and environmental analyses, yet it remains challenging due to their small size and limited size differences. Viscoelastic microfluidics, as a label-free particle manipulation technique, offers promise for the precise separation of small particles. However, the existing viscoelastic microfluidic approaches rely on high polymer concentrations and are limited by low flow rate and throughput. Here, we present a novel hyaluronic acid (HA)-based viscoelastic–Newtonian co-flow microfluidic system that achieves high-throughput separation of algae and bacteria at an ultra-low HA loading concentration. We studied the effects of flow rate ratio, total flow rate, polymer concentration and channel length on the lateral migration of particles in this viscoelastic-Newtonian co-flow system. By optimising the flow parameters and HA concentration (25 ppm), the system can induce selective lateral migration of particles to the Newtonian medium, enabling separation of 1 µm and 5 µm particles. The developed viscoelastic platform is expected to provide simple, high-throughput cell separation and washing, with broad applicability in biology, medicine, and environmental analysis.

Micropipette integrated with exchangeable membrane-pump chips for imaging-guided single-cell isolation
abstract: Micropipetting provides a technological basis for single-cell analysis that preserves cell-specific behavioral information, thereby enabling imaging-guided single-cell isolation. However, broad applicability across diverse cell sizes and motilities remains constrained by the challenge of fast and precise flow control. Here, we present a piezo-driven micropipette integrated with exchangeable membrane-pump chips that enables selection of the controllable-volume range through chip replacement and provides tunable volumetric control with resolutions of 0.15, 0.60, and 1.50 pL and response times on the order of 10 ms. Using this platform, we achieved single-cell isolation with high viability exceeding 90% for motile microalgae ranging from Euglena gracilis to Volvox carteri . We further combined live-cell imaging of antibody secretion activity, micropipette-based isolation, and downstream RT-qPCR for hybridoma and Jurkat cells. This platform provides a route to link dynamic cellular phenotypes with downstream molecular analysis in the same cell.

Humidity-dependent surface chemistry of Au@SnO2 core-shell nanospheres revealed by in situ DRIFTS for H2 and CO sensing
abstract: The dynamic evolution of surface reactions in semiconducting metal oxides (SMOs) under humid conditions remains insufficiently understood. Herein, Au@SnO2 core-shell nanospheres (NS) with tunable SnO2 crystallite sizes were constructed to investigate the humidity-dependent surface chemistry of gas sensing reactions. The Au core provides catalytic activation and interfacial electronic modulation, while the crystallite size and grain-boundary structure of the SnO2 shell regulate the evolution of surface oxygen species, hydroxyl groups, and reaction intermediates. Spectroscopic analyses revealed that H2 sensing was primarily governed by the consumption of adsorbed oxygen species and was therefore strongly suppressed by humidity. In contrast, CO oxidation involved hydroxyl participation and carbonate formation, resulting in distinct humidity-dependent reaction pathways that varied with the shell structure. The CS1-Au@SnO2 NS exhibited sensor responses of 953.5 toward 500 ppm H2 and 87.3 toward 100 ppm CO at 400 °C under 5% relative humidity (RH), with response times below 3 s, whereas the CS3-Au@SnO2 NS maintained a sensor response of 28.2 toward 100 ppm CO even under 75% RH.

3D-printed integrated device including functional paper components for direct Amitraz determination in beehive matrices
abstract: A 3D-printed electroanalytical device (3DD) designed to support the complete analysis of Amitraz (AMZ) is presented. AMZ is a broad-spectrum pesticide widely used to control Varroa destructor in bee colonies. It persists in the environment and in bee products, posing health risks. 3DD functions as a portable laboratory with multiple functional zones connected by microchannels. The device supports direct sampling, automates hydrolysis, and integrates electrochemical measurement. The 3DD body houses a functional rotary valve, into which the untreated sample is inserted. AMZ is converted to 2,4-dimethylaniline (2,4-DMA) via paper-mediated hydrolysis; 2,4-DMA is then flow-transported to the measuring chamber equipped with a paper sensor, where the aniline amine group is oxidized via differential pulse voltammetry (DPV). Disposable paper components enable device reuse. To achieve the required electroanalytical performance, several common and recycled paper substrates and various conductive inks were tested, demonstrating the effectiveness of the paper-mediated hydrolysis process. 3DD integrated AMZ analysis showed useful analytical performance, with a wide linear range (0.05–100 μM), a nanomolar limit of detection (LOD = 14 nM), and reproducibility (RSD ≤ 7%; n = 3). The exploitability of 3DD was demonstrated in both blanks and artificially contaminated honey and beeswax samples, yielding quantitative and reproducible recoveries (96%-112%; RSD ≤ 12%, n = 3). Summing up, we present a device for complete in situ analysis of AMZ. It encompasses all analytical steps, enabling pesticide determination within 5 min without sample pretreatment and highlighting the potential of combining additive manufacturing with functional paper components.

Fluorescent sensor for methyl iodide based on fully conjugated covalent organic framework materials
abstract: A conjugated covalent organic framework (COF), NKCOF-41, was developed as a fluorescent sensor for methyl iodide (CH₃I), representing the first COF-based platform for fluorescent CH₃I detection. The framework was rationally designed with pyridine recognition sites aligned along one-dimensional channels, enabling highly selective binding of CH₃I and efficient fluorescence quenching. Consequently, NKCOF-41 enables sensitive and selective detection of CH₃I in both gas and liquid phases. NKCOF-41 exhibits excellent chemical and structural stability under harsh conditions, including strongly acidic and alkaline environments as well as irradiation. Notably, the material can be processed into solid-state sensing elements (10 mm in diameter and 2 mm in thickness), demonstrating practical applicability for real-world sensing. In solution, the fluorescence intensity of NKCOF-41 decreases by approximately 80% upon addition of 40 μM CH₃I. A linear response between fluorescence intensity and CH₃I concentration was observed over the range of 0–25 μM, with a detection limit of 7.1 nM. This work establishes a COF-based fluorescence sensing strategy for volatile organic iodine, offering a robust solid-state platform for rapid on-site CH₃I screening with promising potential in nuclear safety and environmental monitoring.

abstract: This paper presents a simulation-based optimization of a CO 2 laser photoacoustic spectroscopy (CO 2 LPAS) system for high-precision pollutant monitoring. Using a cylindrical stainless steel resonant cell, the absorption characteristics of ethylene, benzene, toluene, ammonia, and ozone over the 9.2–10.8 µm spectral window were modeled. The results presented in this paper demonstrate exceptional sensitivity, with simulated limits of quantification (LoQ, S/N=3) of 0.49 ppbV for ethylene and 0.75 ppbV for ammonia (corresponding to LoD values, S/N=1, of 0.163 ppbV and 0.25 ppbV, respectively), supported by a cross-sensitivity matrix for efficient species discrimination. A critical focus of this study is the investigation of vibro-translational ( V - T ) relaxation processes catalyzed by water vapor. It has been shown that relative humidity significantly amplifies the photoacoustic signal, and we propose a second-order polynomial compensation algorithm to maintain measurement accuracy under different environmental conditions. In addition, a finite element model has been developed to analyze the acoustic modes and sound pressure distribution within the resonator. The cell, characterized by a resonant frequency of 564 Hz and a quality factor of 16.1, was found to be primarily limited by background noise rather than intrinsic electronic or thermal noise. These findings provide a robust framework for the development of highly sensitive, real-time gas sensors for environmental and industrial applications.

A highly linear current-mode phase-based differential readout for interdigitated capacitive gas sensors
abstract: Capacitive sensors based on interdigitated electrodes (IDCs) represent a solution for highly sensitive detection of environmental gases, thanks to their strong dependence on dielectric variations induced by analyte adsorption. This work presents an IDC-based gas sensor functionalized with a hydrogel-based sensitive layer, together with a dedicated analog readout circuit. The sensing mechanism relies on the modulation of the effective permittivity of the functional layer upon gas exposure, resulting in capacitance variations in the sub-picofarad range. These variations (to 27 pF, from a baseline of 9 pF) are converted into measurable voltage signals through a differential phase-shift architecture, based on the Second-Generation Voltage Conveyor (VCII), allowing inherent rejection of common-mode electrical disturbances and reduced sensitivity to parasitic effects. Thanks to the intrinsic linear phase response around the operating point, the sensor system achieves a highly linear capacitance-phase-voltage transduction over the experimentally investigated range, with a coefficient of determination of approximately 𝑅 2 = 0 . 9 9 7 , simplifying calibration and improving accuracy. Parametric simulations of a CMOS VCII implementation show a capacitance-to-voltage sensitivity of 1.81 mV/pF and a resolution of 0.019 pF. Experimental results on a PCB prototype, based on the AD844, configured as a VCII, confirm the approach, with sensitivity around 103.31 mV/pF and a minimum detectable capacitance variation of approximately 0.33 pF. Gas sensing experiments demonstrate promising performance for H₂O, O₂, and CO₂ detection, under controlled laboratory conditions, in terms of sensitivity and resolution, confirming the feasibility of the proposed approach as a highly linear laboratory-scale platform for capacitive gas-sensing investigations.

A water-soluble H2O2-activatable NIR fluorescence/photoacoustic probe with viscosity-modulated output for longitudinal imaging of drug-induced liver injury
abstract: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) involves oxidative stress and remodeling of the hepatocellular microenvironment. Here, we designed and evaluated two structurally related near-infrared probes, TNO-1 and TNO-2 . TNO-1 exhibited an aqueous solubility of 0.71 mg mL⁻¹ and responded to H 2 O 2 with a detection limit of 0.094 μM. H 2 O 2 -dependent oxidation generated the phenolic product OH-TNO-1 , producing enhanced long-wavelength fluorescence and photoacoustic signals. OH-TNO-1 retained viscosity-sensitive fluorescence consistent with restriction of intramolecular motion. In cultured cells and APAP-challenged mice, TNO-1 produced increased imaging signals that were attenuated by NAC treatment. Comparative experiments using OH-TNO-1 supported a sequential response model in which H 2 O 2 -dependent activation is followed by viscosity-sensitive modulation of the optical output. These findings establish TNO-1 as a proof-of-concept FL/PA platform for longitudinal imaging of APAP-induced liver injury and therapeutic response. Validation in larger animal cohorts, additional liver-injury models, and quantitative correlation with established injury biomarkers will be required to define its diagnostic performance.

Phase-controlled SnS2/ WO3 gas sensors via hydrothermal and partial oxidation routes
abstract: Heterostructured materials combining metal oxides and transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as promising candidates for advanced gas sensors. The WO₃/SnS₂ system remains scarcely explored despite the excellent individual gas sensing properties of both components. We report the synthesis and characterization of WO₃/SnS₂ heterostructures prepared via a two-step hydrothermal method, in which WO₃ nanostructures served as seeds for controlled SnS₂ growth. Stoichiometric control in the synthesis steps and subsequent partial oxidation by thermal treatments allowed fine-tuning of morphology and phase composition. The sample prepared with a Sn:W molar ratio of 10:1 in the synthesis precursor solution delivered the highest response to 10 ppm NO₂ (defined as the ratio of resistances in presence and absence of NO 2 , R NO2 /R 0 ), reaching 1149 after thermal treatment, while the 1:1 and 2:1 molar ratio samples reached responses of 188 and 223, respectively, outperforming similar oxide/TMD systems reported in the literature. This behavior was attributed to synergistic electronic sensitization across the n-n junction and chemical sensitization promoted by partial oxidation. The materials also displayed notable sensitivity to acetone, suggesting its potential for multi-analyte detection. These results highlight WO₃/SnS₂ heterostructures as a novel and effective platform for low-temperature gas sensing relevant to environmental and workplace safety monitoring.

Solid-state electrochemical sensor for hydrogen isotopes. Part I: Modulating isotopic detection through surface engineering with graphene
abstract: Hydrogen and its isotopes are presented as an interesting alternative to fossil fuels because it is intended to use these species in the field of nuclear fusion, and in fields such as fuel cell technology, among others. To this end, the availability of sensors that can measure these isotopes in-situ and online is a key point for the correct development of these technologies. Electrochemical sensors based on solid-state electrolytes have been proved to be able to operate at elevated temperatures, with great physical and chemical stabilities. In this work, electrochemical sensors were constructed and tested using BaCe0.6Zr0.3Y0.1O3-α electrolytes. To achieve different isotopic responses, a graphene layer was transferred onto the surface of the working electrode. The sensors (with and without graphene) were used in a potentiometric and amperometric configuration at 500 °C. Analyte concentrations in the working electrode ranged from 0.12 to 1 mbar of H2 or D2 in Ar. The presence of graphene produced different sensor responses depending on the isotope. In addition, differences in response and recovery times were also observed, being both higher for the sensors with graphene.

title: Missing-linker-confined Ru-based single-atom nanozymes enable proximity-enhanced dual enzyme catalysis and multimodal signal transduction
Hydrophobically coated lead-free halide perovskite films for humidity-stable and sensitive ammonia detection at room temperature
abstract: Ammonia (NH 3 ) chemiresistors based on lead-free halide perovskites such as vacancy-ordered Cs 2 SnI 6 are attractive for room-temperature sensing, but their electrical response is strongly influenced by humidity, leading to baseline evolution, concentration-sweep hysteresis, and limited reproducibility. In this work, Cs 2 SnI 6 is used as a model system to examine how a hydrophobic polystyrene (PS) overlayer modifies humidity-dependent NH 3 sensing while retaining analyte responsiveness. Cs 2 SnI 6 was synthesized hydrothermally, characterised structurally and chemically, and deposited as a sensing film on indium tin oxide interdigitated electrodes. A PS overlayer was subsequently deposited onto the Cs 2 SnI 6 film. XRD and XPS establish the phase and chemical-state assignment of Cs 2 SnI 6 , while Raman spectroscopy confirms preservation of the characteristic vibrational features after PS deposition. The water contact angle increases from approximately 45° to 140° after PS coating, demonstrating substantially increased surface hydrophobicity. Under 20–60% RH, the pristine device exhibits pronounced humidity- and concentration-history dependence, whereas Cs 2 SnI 6 -PS shows substantially reduced hysteresis in the normalized NH 3 response. Low-concentration measurements give LODs of approximately 2.7 and 1.4 ppm for pristine and PS-coated devices, respectively. The PS-coated device also retains its normalized response during 30-day measurements and 50 rapid exposure/recovery cycles, although measurable evolution of the absolute baseline current remains. These results show that PS surface modification improves the reproducibility and humidity tolerance of Cs 2 SnI 6 NH 3 sensing primarily by modifying the surface/interfacial environment rather than by eliminating absolute baseline-current variation.

title: Enhanced NH3 sensing at room temperature using ZnSnO3 hollow spheres/Ti3C2Tx MXene heterostructure
Recent advances in ZnO nanostructures for gas sensing applications: Design strategies, mechanisms, and performance
abstract: There is a growing demand for monitoring low‑concentration gases and odors in applications such as medical diagnostics, healthcare, mobility systems, indoor environment control, food distribution, elderly care, and infectious‑disease prevention. Semiconductor‑type gas sensors based on metal oxides have been widely used for these purposes, with ZnO recognized as one of the most promising materials owing to its high sensitivity and diverse nanostructuring capability. This review summarizes recent advances in ZnO nanostructures for gas sensing, with a focus on strategies for morphology control, crystal‑facet engineering, and defect modulation. A wide variety of ZnO nanostructures—such as whiskers, nanowires, plates, rods, spheres, nanosheets, and self‑assembled films—have been developed to enhance gas adsorption, charge‑transfer efficiency, and selective reactivity toward specific gases. Structural features at both the nanoscale and atomic scale, including surface defects, kinks, steps, and metastable crystal facets, have been reported to be strongly associated with sensing performance. The review also discusses remaining challenges for practical implementation, including humidity robustness, concentration-matched selectivity, long-term stability, reproducibility, low-power operation, and standardized performance reporting. The unique physicochemical characteristics of these ZnO nanostructures enable the detection of trace‑level gases and odors, highlighting the potential of ZnO‑based sensors for next‑generation environmental and biological monitoring.

Dual-readout cerium oxide nanoparticle paper-based sensors for redox profiling via hydrogen peroxide detection in 2D and 3D chronic lymphocytic leukemia models
abstract: A low-cost paper-based analytical device (PAD) was developed for rapid dual detection, integrating an electrochemical PAD (ePAD), which is turbidity-independent, and a smartphone-assisted optical/colorimetric PAD (oPAD). Both platforms employ cerium oxide nanoparticles (nCe) as enzyme-free nanozymes for H₂O₂ detection in 2D and 3D chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) models. The system enables rapid analysis (<1 min) using only 5 µL of sample and exhibits excellent operational stability.The ePAD shows a wide linear range (3 nM–500 µM) with an ultralow detection limit of 0.4 nM, while the oPAD exhibits a detection limit of 0.3 µM within a 1–1000 µM range, both covering physiologically relevant H₂O₂ concentrations. Validation in both 2D cultures and, notably, in 3D CLL co-culture systems incorporating stromal cells—mimicking the architecture and biochemical gradients of the in vivo microenvironment and enhancing cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions—demonstrates the device’s capability to monitor redox dynamics under biologically relevant conditions.Owing to its high sensitivity, low sample requirement, and complementary electrochemical and optical readouts, the nCe-PAD represents a versatile platform for real-time redox profiling, early assessment of oxidative stress, and personalized monitoring in complex tumor microenvironment models, paving the way toward robust point-of-care analytical solutions for redox-related pathologies.

Protonation-governed dual-emission nitrogen-doped carbon dots for differential fluorescence modulation to tetracycline antibiotics
abstract: The fluorescence response of carbon-dot-based sensing systems is commonly interpreted in terms of analyte-induced quenching or enhancement, while the role of protonation equilibria and interfacial pH dynamics are often underestimated. Here, electrochemically synthesized nitrogen-doped carbon dots (N-CDs) exhibiting excitation-dependent dual emission were investigated for the detection and differential recognition of tetracycline antibiotics under buffered and unbuffered aqueous environments. Fluorescence modulation in the N-CDs–tetracyclines system was influenced by coupled protonation equilibria involving both the amphoteric antibiotics and the N-CDs surface states. Under alkaline conditions, tetracycline induced fluorescence attenuation at both excitation wavelengths (λ ex = 350 and 410 nm), whereas chlortetracycline produced a dual response consisting of quenching at 410 nm excitation and pronounced enhancement at 350 nm excitation, enabling differential recognition of structurally related antibiotics. Comparative studies under controlled and uncontrolled pH conditions revealed that analyte-induced pH variations contribute to the observed fluorescence changes, introducing a source of mechanistic ambiguity in conventional sensing interpretations. Fluorescence lifetime, ζ-potential, and UV–vis analyses indicated that the observed response arises from the coupled contributions involving pH-dependent analyte speciation, N-CDs surface protonation, inner filter effects, and adsorption-mediated interactions. Importantly, chlortetracycline enhancement involved not only modulation of N-CDs fluorescence but also its intrinsic fluorescence, favoured by pH-dependent speciation in the alkaline N-CDs microenvironment. Exploiting these mechanistic differences enabled wavelength-resolved differential recognition of tetracyclines and proof-of-concept micromolar detection in tap and river water. These findings establish protonation dynamics as a critical parameter in carbon-dot sensing systems and provide mechanistic guidance for interpretation in complex aqueous matrices.

Porphyrin optical transducer for ion-selective optodes operating in highly acidic range
abstract: An approach is proposed that allows the application of ion-selective optodes in highly acidic media. For the first time, a free base porphyrin is used as the optical transducer in ion-selective sensors. Protonation/deprotonation of the porphyrin is associated with a change in the color and emission spectra. For protonated porphyrin molecules embedded in plasticized PVC-based ion-selective membrane, binding of primary cations to ionophore results in deprotonation of the dye to maintain electroneutrality of the membrane bulk. This process is observed as an increase in emission intensity for the increase in cations concentration in the sample, yielding a fluorescence turn-on ion-selective optical response. The porphyrin deprotonation is accompanied by a color change of the PVC film, from green in the absence of the analyte, to pink allowing application of porphyrin optical transducer in ion-selective colorimetric sensors. Both changes in red and blue color intensity are linearly dependent on the change in the logarithm of the analyte ions concentration in the solution. The porphyrin-based optode is reversible in both emission and colorimetric modes. The important advantage of using a free base porphyrin as an optical transducer in ion selective sensors lies in its potential use of the devices in highly acidic samples, e.g. to monitor release of ions of interest from precipitates, i.e. in the conditions where classical optical transducers cannot be applied.

Characterization of spectroscopic sensing system using waveguide absorption cell with gas diffusion holes
abstract: This paper reports a systematic study of diffusion-based hollow waveguide (HWG) sensor for pump-free operation by strategically drilled gas holes. Through ray-tracing and computational fluid dynamics simulations, the effects of HWG curvature, gas hole location, size, and number on both optical loss and gas diffusion time are quantitatively analyzed. The results clarify that positioning gas holes on the inner side of a bent HWG minimizes optical loss. Furthermore, the configuration employing multiple small holes provides an effective strategy for balancing low optical loss with rapid gas diffusion. HWG samples with varied hole parameters were fabricated and integrated into a spectroscopic sensing system with a broadband infrared source and a tunable Fabry-Pérot (FP) detector. Experiments validated the design approach, with a 15-hole HWG achieving a CO2 diffusion time of 20 s and a limit of detection (LOD) of 385 ppb. This work proposes a portable HWG gas sensor based on free diffusion, demonstrating a viable pathway to fast-response, high-performance sensing without the need for pumps.

title: Open centrifugal microfluidic chip with selective surface modification for droplet-based single-cell granzyme B activity profiling
abstract: Monitoring immune function at the single-cell level is essential for understanding immune heterogeneity and evaluating responses to immunotherapies. Several microfluidic platforms capable of single-cell assays require external equipment and specially trained operators, limiting accessibility and routine laboratory use. This work introduces a simple, pump-free microfluidic platform designed for high-throughput single-cell trapping and functional enzymatic monitoring within isolated microenvironments. We present an open centrifugal microfluidic chip featuring an array of hexagonal microchambers with selectively oxygen-plasma-treated surfaces that enable droplet-based compartmentalization of single cells. Centrifugal actuation drives cell loading, trapping, and droplet formation, thus simplifying the operation. By optimizing loading conditions, the device achieved efficient single-cell occupancy and supported short-term live-cell analysis. Fluorescence calibration using 5-FAM established a detection limit of 3.15 pmol, demonstrating the system’s suitability for single-cell enzymatic analysis. Using PBMCs from healthy donors, the device revealed heterogeneous GzmB activity at the single-cell level and detected increased enzymatic activity following IL-2 stimulation. Immunofluorescence staining enabled the simultaneous identification of immune cell subsets, showing a corresponding increase in the proportion of CD8⁺ T cells. Moreover, its open configuration enables direct retrieval of selected cells for downstream analyses. Our open centrifugal microfluidic chip combines ease of operation, analytical sensitivity, and single-cell resolution to enable comprehensive immune profiling. By revealing functional heterogeneity within immune populations and facilitating downstream cell analysis, it holds significant potential for immune monitoring, disease prognosis, and the development of next-generation precision immunotherapies.

Magnetorheological armor for programmable droplet manipulation
abstract: Magnetically actuated droplets offer a remote, low-resistance route for microscale sample handling in chemical analysis, biomedical testing, and environmental monitoring. Yet practical applications require droplets not only to move reliably, but also to deform for reagent access and analysis while remaining protected from external contamination, which remains difficult when traditional magnetic methods are largely limited to movement control. Here, we report a reconfigurable magnetorheological armor in which magnetic colloids assemble into an external armor layer at the droplet interface. Under magnetic fields, the colloids form chain-like networks that reinforce the interfacial armor, transmit magnetic force, and keep the liquid core additive-free. By tuning field geometry, the armor redistributes across the droplet surface, enabling programmable deformation, on-demand detachment, low-resistance transport, and robust operation on contaminated surfaces, vertical substrates, immiscible liquids, and confined tubing. This field-regulated interface achieved a deformation recovery rate above 97.5%, a motion resistance as low as 0.164 mN, and droplet velocities up to 14.5 mm/s. In a Cu 2 + colorimetric assay, armored droplets underwent protected cross-media transfer, local opening, reagent coalescence, and re-encapsulation, achieving 99.3% colorimetric accuracy. This work turns the droplet surface into a field-programmable interface for actuation, protection, and on-demand analysis.

Integration of molecular imprinting into paper-based electrochemical platforms for on-site ciprofloxacin monitoring
abstract: Ciprofloxacin (CIP), known for its broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and clinical applicability, is among the most detected antibiotics in surface- and wastewaters. This work describes the development of a paper-based electrochemical cell, modified with single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) and a molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP), for the sensitive and selective voltammetric analysis of CIP. The cell features an integrated three-electrode system, fabricated by inkjet printing on waterproof paper. The MIP was produced directly on the working electrode of the cell through electropolymerization of the computationally selected 3-aminophenylboronic acid monomer in the presence of CIP. After optimization of important experimental parameters related to the MIP synthesis (monomer:template ratio, number of polymerization cycles, and incubation time), a linear concentration range of 0.25–20 µmol L −1 was established using differential pulse voltammetry. The MIP paper-based cell revealed limits of detection (LOD) and quantification (LOQ) of 0.066 µmol L −1 and 0.22 µmol L −1 , respectively, using a 7 min incubation with the CIP solution. The sensor exhibited selectivity toward CIP when compared with structurally related or co-occurring pharmaceutical compounds. Its applicability was demonstrated in spiked river- and tap water and validated in wastewater effluents, highlighting its potential for future on-site CIP screening.

GFET-based Optoelectrical Platform for Potassium Blood Testing and Quantification
abstract: Accurate monitoring of blood potassium is critical for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet current methods remain invasive, costly, and poorly suited for frequency testing. Here, we present a proof-of-concept for a graphene field-effect transistor (GFET)-based platform aimed at potassium detection in whole blood. By optimizing a potassium ion-selective membrane, we achieve a higher sensitivity of 154.72 μ A/decade and high reproducibility (ICC - 0.70, RSD = 0.63%). To adapt our system towards a single-chip platform, we integrated a saturated KCl hydrogel pseudo-reference electrode onto the GFET platform. This preserved sensor performance relevant to a commercial Ag/AgCl electrode. To mitigate haemolysis-induced error in small-volume samples, we further trialled a cuvette-based GFET platform coupled with a custom 805 nm optical module. This dual-modal system demonstrated the feasibility simultaneous electrochemical quantification of total potassium and optical estimation of intracellular potassium contribution. The combined approach demonstrates a promising pathway towards minimally invasive, point-of-care potassium monitoring.
